quotation.text: I shall quote again the words narrated by Moses himself, from which we can indisputably learn that [God] conversed with some one who was numerically distinct from Himself, and also a rational Being.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Justin argues from Genesis 1:26 and Genesis 3:22 that God was speaking to another person, numerically distinct from himself and rational, whom Justin identifies with the Offspring begotten from the Father before all creatures.

explanation: In Dialogue 62 Justin answers Trypho's teachers, who said God spoke to himself, or to the elements from which man was formed, when he said 'Let us make man.' Justin replies that Moses shows God conversing with someone numerically distinct and rational, and he identifies that someone with the Offspring truly brought forth from the Father, who was with the Father before all creatures and is the Wisdom of Proverbs 8.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (standards section 2, row C): Justin reads the plural of Genesis 1:26 as God the Father speaking to the Son/Word. The Genesis text itself (row A) does not name Father, Son, or Holy Spirit and does not state the later doctrine of the Trinity; Justin's inference (row B) that the addressee is the pre-existent Word is his own, and the later Nicene formulation (row D, 325) must not be projected back onto him.
historicalContext: Dialogue with Trypho, written c. 155-160 (range), is Justin's defence of Christianity in dialogue with the Jew Trypho, arguing from the Old Testament that Jesus is the Christ and is divine. The chapters cited here (56, 62) belong to the section in which Justin argues that the Scriptures speak of another God and Lord, distinct from the Maker yet subject to him.
citation: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 62, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01285.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: Moses, then, the blessed and faithful servant of God, declares that He who appeared to Abraham under the oak in Mamre is God, sent with the two angels in His company to judge Sodom by Another who remains ever in the supercelestial places, invisible to all men, holding personal intercourse with none, whom we believe to be Maker and Father of all things
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Justin reads the three visitors at Mamre as God himself appearing with two angels, sent by the Father who remains in heaven.

explanation: Justin argues that the one who appeared to Abraham at Mamre (Gen 18:1) is God, yet distinct from the Father, who remains in the supercelestial places and holds personal intercourse with none. The visible God who appears and speaks is, for Justin, the Son/Word, sent by the Father to judge Sodom.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Justin reads Genesis 18:1 as a theophany of the Son, distinct from the Father. The text itself (row A) says the LORD appeared to Abraham, without distinguishing persons; the identification of the visible God with the Son is Justin's reading, not the text's explicit statement, and it is not the later Nicene doctrine (row D).
historicalContext: Dialogue with Trypho, written c. 155-160 (range), is Justin's defence of Christianity in dialogue with the Jew Trypho, arguing from the Old Testament that Jesus is the Christ and is divine. The chapters cited here (56, 62) belong to the section in which Justin argues that the Scriptures speak of another God and Lord, distinct from the Maker yet subject to him.
citation: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 56, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01285.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: And He is the Lord who received commission from the Lord who [remains] in the heavens, i.e., the Maker of all things, to inflict upon Sodom and Gomorrha the [judgments] which the Scripture describes in these terms: 'The Lord rained down upon Sodom and Gomorrha sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven.'
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Justin reads 'the LORD rained... from the LORD' as two Lords: the Lord on earth who judged Sodom, commissioned by the Lord in heaven, the Maker.

explanation: Justin argues that the Lord who rained fire on Sodom is the same God who appeared to Abraham, and that he received his commission from the Lord who remains in heaven. For Justin this shows Scripture itself speaking of one who is called Lord and God besides the Maker of all things, yet subject to him: 'another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things.'
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Justin reads Genesis 19:24 as the Son receiving a commission from the Father to judge Sodom. The text itself (row A) says the LORD rained fire from the LORD; the identification of the two Lords as Son and Father is Justin's reading. His language of 'another God and Lord subject to the Maker' is recorded as he wrote it and must not be harmonised into later Nicene equality (row D).
historicalContext: Dialogue with Trypho, written c. 155-160 (range), is Justin's defence of Christianity in dialogue with the Jew Trypho, arguing from the Old Testament that Jesus is the Christ and is divine. The chapters cited here (56, 62) belong to the section in which Justin argues that the Scriptures speak of another God and Lord, distinct from the Maker yet subject to him.
citation: Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho, ch. 56, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01285.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: For with Him were always present the Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, by whom and in whom, freely and spontaneously, He made all things, to whom also He speaks, saying, Let Us make man after Our image and likeness
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Irenaeus reads 'Let us make man' as God the Father speaking to the Word and Wisdom - the Son and the Spirit - who were always present with him and are his 'hands' in creation.

explanation: Against the claim that angels made man, Irenaeus argues in IV.20 that God needed no angels: the Word and Wisdom, Son and Spirit, were always with him, and to them he spoke 'Let us make man.' Man was formed by God's hands, that is, by the Son and Holy Spirit. The preface to Book IV states the same point: man was 'moulded by His hands, that is, by the Son and Holy Spirit, to whom also He said, Let Us make man.'
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Irenaeus identifies the addressees of Genesis 1:26 as Son and Spirit. The text (row A) gives only the plural; the identification is Irenaeus's reading, and his 'two hands' imagery is his own, not later Nicene vocabulary (row D).
historicalContext: Against Heresies, written c. 175-185 (range), is Irenaeus's refutation of Valentinian Gnosticism. Book III argues from Scripture that the Creator is the one true God and Father of Jesus Christ; Book IV argues that the one God formed all things by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit.
citation: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, IV.20.1, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103420.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrha fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven. For it here points out that the Son, who had also been talking with Abraham, had received power to judge the Sodomites for their wickedness.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Irenaeus reads Genesis 19:24 as the Son, who had talked with Abraham, receiving power from the Father to judge Sodom.

explanation: In the same passage as his Psalm 110:1 argument, Irenaeus cites the destruction of Sodom: the Son, who had also been talking with Abraham, received power to judge the Sodomites. The two 'Lords' of the verse are, for Irenaeus, the Father in heaven and the Son who executes judgment.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Irenaeus reads Genesis 19:24 as the Son judging Sodom by power received from the Father. The text itself (row A) says the LORD rained fire from the LORD; the Father/Son identification is Irenaeus's reading, and it is not the later Nicene doctrine (row D).
historicalContext: Against Heresies, written c. 175-185 (range), is Irenaeus's refutation of Valentinian Gnosticism. Book III argues from Scripture that the Creator is the one true God and Father of Jesus Christ; Book IV argues that the one God formed all things by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit.
citation: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, III.6.1, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103306.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: In like manner also the three days which were before the luminaries, are types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom. And the fourth is the type of man, who needs light, that so there may be God, the Word, wisdom, man.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Commenting on the creation days of Genesis 1, Theophilus calls the three days before the sun and moon 'types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom' - using the word Trinity (Greek Trias) of God, his Word, and his Wisdom.

explanation: In To Autolycus II.15 Theophilus allegorises the fourth day: the sun is a type of God and the moon of man, while the three days before the luminaries prefigure the Trinity - God, his Word, and his Wisdom. His 'Trinity' is God, Word, and Wisdom; he does not name the Holy Spirit here, and Wisdom is elsewhere in his work also a title of the Son.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Theophilus reads the Genesis 1 creation days typologically. The Genesis text (row A) says nothing of a Trinity; the typology is Theophilus's, and his triad of God, Word, and Wisdom is not the later Nicene Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (row D) - the difference must be stated, not smoothed over.
historicalContext: To Autolycus, written c. 180 (approximate), is Theophilus's apology addressed to his pagan friend Autolycus. Book II walks through Genesis 1 day by day with allegorising commentary, and explains how the uncontainable Father can be said to walk in Paradise (ch. 22).
citation: Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, II.15, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02042.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: Secondary literature commonly describes this as the earliest surviving Christian use of the word 'Trinity' (Greek Trias); that claim was not independently verified in this pass.

quotation.text: Moreover, God is found, as if needing help, to say, Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness. But to no one else than to His own Word and wisdom did He say, Let Us make.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Theophilus reads 'Let us make man' as God speaking to no one else than his own Word and Wisdom.

explanation: In II.18 Theophilus says God made all things by his Word, and reckons the creation of man the only work worthy of his own hands; the plural 'Let us make' is addressed to his Word and Wisdom alone, as if God needed help.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Theophilus identifies the addressees of Genesis 1:26 as God's own Word and Wisdom. The text (row A) gives only the plural; the identification is Theophilus's reading, and his Word/Wisdom pair is not later Nicene Father/Son/Spirit language (row D).
historicalContext: To Autolycus, written c. 180 (approximate), is Theophilus's apology addressed to his pagan friend Autolycus. Book II walks through Genesis 1 day by day with allegorising commentary, and explains how the uncontainable Father can be said to walk in Paradise (ch. 22).
citation: Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, II.18, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02042.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: Theophilus's pair is Word and Wisdom; he does not name the Holy Spirit in this passage.

quotation.text: Nay, it was because He had already His Son close at His side, as a second Person, His own Word, and a third Person also, the Spirit in the Word, that He purposely adopted the plural phrase, “Let us make;” and, “in our image;” and, “become as one of us.”
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3 (1885)

explanation: Tertullian argues that the plural 'Let us make' in Genesis 1:26 cannot be God speaking to angels (the Jewish reading he rejects) or God speaking to himself as a solitary being; it is God speaking with the Son already at his side as a second Person and the Spirit as a third Person. The plural is therefore, for Tertullian, evidence of a plurality of Persons in the Godhead.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Tertullian reads Genesis 1:26 as the Father speaking to the Son and the Spirit, and so as proof of the plurality of Persons. (A) The text itself does not name Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and does not state the Trinity; Tertullian's reading is reception history, not the text's plain meaning. (D) Tertullian's language is pre-Nicene: he speaks of three Persons of one substance, but he does not use or teach Nicaea's homoousios, and his Son is in some respects subordinate (a portion of the Father's substance, proceeding for the work of creation).
historicalContext: Against Praxeas was written c. 207-213 (range), in Tertullian's Montanist period, against Praxeas, who taught that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same Person. The treatise is the earliest Latin work to use trinitas (Trinity) and persona (Person) as theological terms.
citation: Tertullian, Against Praxeas. Translated by Peter Holmes. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3, ed. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/tertullian/against_praxeas/anf03.v.ix.ii.html (ch. 2); https://ccel.org/ccel/tertullian/against_praxeas/anf03.v.ix.xii.html (ch. 12).
notes: No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task. Tertullian also records the reading he rejects, that God spoke to the angels; that rejected reading is described in the explanation above.

quotation.text: Certainly, in that it is of the plural number, the word our would not be rightly used if man were made in the image of one person, whether of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit; but because he was made in the image of the Trinity, on that account it is said, After our image.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine argues that the plural 'our' in 'Let us make man in our image' (Gen. 1:26) shows man was made in the image of the Trinity, not of one person alone.

explanation: Augustine is rejecting the opinion that the image of the Trinity in man is completed in husband, wife, and offspring. He argues from the plural 'our' in Genesis 1:26 that man was made in the image of the whole Trinity, and from the singular 'God created man in the image of God' (Gen. 1:27) that the Trinity is one God, not three Gods.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads the plural 'let us make' / 'our image' in Genesis 1:26 as showing that man was made in the image of the Trinity. (A) The text itself names no persons and does not state the doctrine; Augustine's reading is reception history, not the text's plain meaning. (B) The step from the unexplained plural to a trinitarian referent is Augustine's inference. (D) The formulated doctrine of one essence in three persons dates from later centuries and is not read back into the verse.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book XII, where Augustine seeks the image of God in the mind and rejects a marital/offspring image of the Trinity.
citation: Augustine, On the Holy Trinity (De Trinitate), in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff, trans. Arthur West Haddan (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887), Book 12, ch. 6, section 6. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/130112.htm
notes: Augustine's psychological analogies (memory, understanding, will; De Trinitate Books IX-X, XIV-XV) are his own reading (C), not the biblical text's meaning. Alternative readings of the plural (plural of majesty, heavenly court) are not addressed by Augustine here; they are recorded in the passage record, not suppressed.

quotation.text: But since three men appeared, and no one of them is said to be greater than the rest either in form, or age, or power, why should we not here understand, as visibly intimated by the visible creature, the equality of the Trinity, and one and the same substance in three persons?
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine argues that because three men of equal standing appeared to Abraham, the scene visibly intimates the equality of the Trinity and one substance in three persons.

explanation: Augustine is asking whether God the Trinity, or one person of the Trinity, appeared to the fathers. Of the Mamre visitation he notes that Scripture first says 'The Lord appeared to him' and then tells of three men whom Abraham addresses in the singular as one Lord; since no one of the three is said to be greater, he reads the scene as a visible intimation of the Trinity's equality and one substance.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads the three visitors at Mamre as visibly intimating the equality of the Trinity and one substance in three persons. (A) The Genesis text calls the visitors men and the LORD, names no persons of the Trinity, and does not state the doctrine. (B) The step from 'three men, none greater' to the Trinity is Augustine's inference. (D) The formulated doctrine is later and is not projected back onto the narrative.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book II, chapters 10-11, where Augustine examines the theophanies to the fathers to show that the Trinity works indivisibly in each appearance and that being sent or appearing does not imply inferiority.
citation: Augustine, On the Holy Trinity (De Trinitate), in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff, trans. Arthur West Haddan (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887), Book 2, ch. 11, section 20. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/130102.htm
notes: Augustine himself notes the uncertainty: in II.10.19 he says it 'does not appear plainly whether it was any person of the Trinity that appeared to Abraham, or God Himself the Trinity.' His conclusion in II.11.20 is framed as a question ('why should we not here understand...'), not as a certainty.

quotation.text: But now the writer of the Book, not saying this indeed, but allotting the creation to the plural number and adding Our image, well-nigh with clear and mighty voice proclaims the enumeration of the Holy Trinity to be above One.
quotation.edition: P. E. Pusey edition/translation (Oxford, 1872), as reproduced at elpenor.org
quotation.location: Book I, on John 1:1 (elpenor Part 1, p. 10)
quotation.summary: Cyril argues that Genesis 1:26, by allotting creation to the plural number and adding 'Our image', proclaims the enumeration of the Holy Trinity to be above One.

explanation: Cyril is opening his commentary on John 1:1 and answering the question who created the world. He cites Genesis 1:26, where God says 'Let us make man in our image', and argues that the plural 'Let us' and 'Our image' shows that the work of creation is not the Father's alone but is shared with the Son and the Holy Spirit - the Holy Trinity, 'above One'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Cyril reads the plural 'Let us make' / 'Our image' in Genesis 1:26 as proclaiming the enumeration of the Holy Trinity to be above One. (A) The Genesis text names no persons and does not state the doctrine; it speaks of God in the plural. (B) The step from the unexplained plural to the Trinity is Cyril's inference. (D) The formulated doctrine is later and is not read back into the verse.
historicalContext: The Commentary on the Gospel according to John was written 425-428 (range), before the outbreak of the Nestorian controversy. Cyril argues throughout against Arian and Eunomian teaching about the Son and the Holy Spirit.
citation: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel according to John, trans. P. E. Pusey, 3 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1872), Book I, on John 1:1. https://www.elpenor.org/cyril-alexandria/john-commentary.asp?pg=10
notes: Cyril does not address alternative readings of the plural (plural of majesty, heavenly court); they are recorded in the passage record, not suppressed.

quotation.text: it is by no means an obscure testimony which Moses bears in the history of the creation, when he says that the Spirit of God was expanded over the abyss or shapeless matter; for it shows not only that the beauty which the world displays is maintained by the invigorating power of the Spirit, but that even before this beauty existed the Spirit was at work cherishing the confused mass.
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 14
quotation.summary: Calvin reads Genesis 1:1-2 as showing the Spirit at work before the world's beauty existed, and therefore as eternal rather than created.

explanation: Calvin cites the Spirit of God moving over the waters (Genesis 1:2, within the creation account of Genesis 1:1) as a testimony to the Spirit's deity: the Spirit was already at work cherishing the formless mass before the beauty of the world existed, and the world's beauty is still maintained by his invigorating power. Because the Spirit acts before creation is ordered, Calvin holds that the Spirit is not a creature but eternal.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Genesis 1:1-2 as showing the Spirit's pre-creation activity, and therefore his eternity. (A) The text says the Spirit of God was over the waters before the world was ordered. (B) The inference from pre-creation activity to eternity is Calvin's. (D) 'Person' and 'deity' are later doctrinal terms applied to the text.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.14, final edition 1559. Calvin is proving the deity of the Holy Spirit from Old Testament passages; Genesis 1:1-2 is his first exhibit in the section.
citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, section 14. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: The quotation is a clause of a longer sentence in Beveridge's translation, quoted from its start ('it is by no means an obscure testimony...'); the wording 'expanded over' is Beveridge's rendering of the Hebrew as printed on the checked page. No attested dissenting reading of Genesis 1:1 was located in the era sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 33, a. 3, respondeo, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1033.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas argues that 'Father' is applied to God first as a personal name (the Father of the Son from eternity) and only secondarily as an essential name (God as Father of creatures). He illustrates the secondary, creaturely sense with Deuteronomy 32:6: God is called Father of the rational creature 'by reason of the likeness of His image', because He possessed, made, and created them. The verse is used for the creaturely, not the intra-Trinitarian, sense of fatherhood.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article treats the person of the Father (q. 33) and distinguishes personal from essential uses of 'Father'.
notes: Aquinas cites Deuteronomy 32:6 in the Douay wording ('who possessed, and made, and created thee'); the ESV renders 'your father, who created you'. The wording difference does not affect the point recorded here.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 33, a. 3, respondeo
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites Deuteronomy 32:6 for God as Father of the rational creature by likeness of image, as the secondary (creaturely) sense of 'Father', distinct from the personal sense of Father of the Son.
quotation.text: Of some, namely, the rational creature (He is the Father), by reason of the likeness of His image, according to Deuteronomy 32:6: "Is He not thy Father, who possessed, and made, and created thee?"
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads Deuteronomy 32:6 as speaking of God's fatherhood toward the rational creature, by likeness of image, and explicitly distinguishes this from the personal sense in which the Father is Father of the Son. (A) The text calls God Israel's father as creator and founder of the nation; it does not name the Father as a distinct divine person. (D) The distinction between personal and essential uses of 'Father' is Aquinas's scholastic formulation and must not be read back into the Song of Moses.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 39, a. 3, sed contra, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1039.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether essential names should be predicated of the three persons in the singular or the plural. Against the claim that the three persons are 'three Gods', he cites Deuteronomy 6:4 ('Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God') as the authority that the one divine essence is predicated in the singular. The Shema is, for Aquinas, the scriptural ground for saying 'one God' rather than 'three Gods'.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article belongs to Aquinas's treatment of the persons in relation to the essence (q. 39), addressing the grammar of divine names.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 39, a. 3, sed contra
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites Deuteronomy 6:4 against saying the three persons are 'three Gods': the Lord God is one God.
quotation.text: It is said (Deuteronomy 6:4): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God."
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads Deuteronomy 6:4 as the scriptural authority for predicating 'God' of the three persons in the singular: one God, not three Gods. (A) The text states that the LORD is one; it says nothing about three persons or about the later doctrine. (D) The scholastic question of singular versus plural predication of essential names is a thirteenth-century formulation; the Shema supplies the 'one God' premise, and the 'three persons' half of the doctrine comes from elsewhere.

quotation.text: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make Your enemies Your footstool. Here the [Scripture] represents to us the Father addressing the Son; He who gave Him the inheritance of the heathen, and subjected to Him all His enemies.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Irenaeus reads Psalm 110:1 as the Father addressing the Son, giving him the inheritance of the nations and subjecting his enemies to him.

explanation: Against Heresies III.6 argues that Scripture never calls anyone God or Lord absolutely except the true God - the Father ruling over all and his Son who has received dominion from the Father. Psalm 110:1 is Irenaeus's first proof: the Father speaks to the Son as 'my Lord.' Since both Father and Son are truly Lord, the Holy Spirit has fitly designated them by the title of Lord.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Irenaeus reads Psalm 110:1 as the Father addressing the Son. The psalm itself (row A) is a royal psalm in which God speaks to a lord at his right hand; the identification of the speakers as Father and Son is Irenaeus's reading, directed against Gnostic claims of other gods, and it is not the later Nicene formulation (row D).
historicalContext: Against Heresies, written c. 175-185 (range), is Irenaeus's refutation of Valentinian Gnosticism. explanation: Aquinas asks whether any procession in God can be called generation. Against the objection that generation involves change from non-existence to existence, he cites Psalm 2:7, 'This day have I begotten Thee', as the scriptural authority that the procession of the Word is called generation. In his respondeo he argues that the Word proceeds by way of similitude in the same nature, so that this procession is properly generation and the Word is properly called Son.

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads Psalm 2:7 as the scriptural warrant for calling the Word's procession 'generation' and the Word 'Son'. (B) The step from the psalm's enthronement language to an eternal generation is an inference, which Aquinas supports by his scholastic account of the Word as proceeding by way of similitude in the same nature. quotation.text: When it is said in the forty-fifth Psalm, 'Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever,' the Jews quibble that the name Elohim is applied to angels and sovereign powers. But no passage is to be found in Scripture, where an eternal throne is set up for a creature.

quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 9
quotation.summary: Calvin argues that Psalm 45:6 addresses the king as God and gives him an eternal throne, which no creature possesses, so the verse proves the deity of Christ.

explanation: Calvin cites Psalm 45:6 as a proof of Christ's deity: the psalm addresses the king as 'God' and gives him a throne 'for ever and ever', and no passage of Scripture sets up an eternal throne for a creature. He anticipates the objection that 'Elohim' is sometimes applied to angels and rulers, and answers that the eternal throne distinguishes this use. The verse is used, in the context of Institutes I.xiii.9, as one of a series of Old Testament testimonies to the Son's deity (with Isaiah 9:6).
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Psalm 45:6 as a divine address to Christ, proving his deity. (A) The text addresses the king as 'God' and gives him an eternal throne. (B) The inference that the addressee is therefore God by nature is Calvin's, resting on the eternity of the throne. (D) The identification of the addressee with Christ, and the term 'deity', are doctrinal applications, not the psalm's own wording.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.9, final edition 1559. Calvin is assembling Old Testament proofs of the Son's deity; his phrase 'the Jews quibble' is his own polemical wording against a contemporary Jewish reading of the verse, recorded here as he wrote it.

explanation: Aquinas asks whether a divine person is sent only by the person whence He proceeds eternally. Against that view he cites Isaiah 48:16: 'Now the Lord God hath sent Me and His Spirit' — the Son is sent by the Holy Ghost, although the Son does not proceed from the Holy Ghost. Aquinas resolves the difficulty by distinguishing two senses of 'sending': as designating the principle of the person sent, a person is sent only by the one whence He proceeds; as designating the principle of the effect implied in the mission, the whole Trinity sends the person sent.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article closes q. 43 on the mission of the divine persons, drawing on Augustine's De Trinitate II and IV.
notes: Aquinas cites Isaiah 48:16 in the Douay wording ('Now the Lord God hath sent Me and His Spirit'); the ESV renders 'the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit'. The identity of the speaker ('me') is not stated in the verse; Aquinas reads the speaker as the Son.

(D) The mission/procession distinction is Aquinas's scholastic formulation and must not be presented as the wording of Isaiah 48:16.

quotation.text: Again, no cavils can explain away the force of what Isaiah says, 'And now the Lord God, and his Spirit, has sent me,' thus ascribing a share in the sovereign power of sending the prophets to the Holy Spirit.

quotation.summary: Calvin reads Isaiah 48:16 as ascribing to the Holy Spirit a share in the sovereign power of sending the prophets, which belongs to God alone.

explanation: Calvin cites Isaiah 48:16 ('And now the Lord God, and his Spirit, has sent me') as a proof of the Spirit's deity: sending the prophets is a sovereign power that belongs to God, and the verse ascribes a share in that power to the Spirit, who is therefore God and not a creature. The argument is one of a series in Institutes I.xiii.14 for the Spirit's deity, alongside Genesis 1:1-2.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Isaiah 48:16 as ascribing a divine prerogative (sending the prophets) to the Holy Spirit. (A) The text says the Lord God and his Spirit have sent the speaker. (B) The inference that sharing in sending proves the Spirit's deity is Calvin's. (D) The doctrinal terms 'deity' and 'person' are later vocabulary applied to the text.

quotation.summary: Justin describes Christian baptism as washing in the name of God the Father, Jesus Christ the Saviour, and the Holy Spirit - the threefold name of Matthew 28:19 as practised in his community.

explanation: In First Apology 61 Justin explains baptism to the emperor: converts who believe and repent are brought to water and 'regenerated' in the threefold name. He presents this as the practice learned from the apostles, and adds that the name of God the Father, the name of Jesus Christ, and the name of the Holy Ghost are pronounced over the one being washed.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Justin's baptismal practice uses the threefold name of Matthew 28:19. The passage itself (row A) is the risen Jesus' commission to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; Justin's report is evidence about second-century baptismal practice and belief, not a doctrinal treatise, and he uses no later Trinitarian terminology (row D).
historicalContext: First Apology, written c. 150-155 (range) and addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius, defends Christians against charges of atheism and immorality and describes Christian worship, including baptism (ch. 61) and the refutation of atheism (ch. 6).

explanation: In stating the rule of faith, Tertullian names the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost together as the objects of Christian belief, and describes the Spirit as sent from heaven from the Father to sanctify the faith of believers. He then states the formula that the dispensation 'distributes the Unity into a Trinity, placing in their order the three Persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost', yet of one substance, one condition, and one power.

(D) Tertullian's 'one substance, three Persons' is the Latin formula that later fed into Nicene theology, but Tertullian himself predates Nicaea by over a century and does not teach homoousios.

(A) The text commands baptism in the name (singular) of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; it does not use the word Trinity or state a doctrine of one essence. quotation.text: And Christ was certainly not then anointed with the Holy Spirit, when He, as a dove, descended upon Him at His baptism. For at that time He deigned to prefigure His body, i.e. His Church, in which especially the baptized receive the Holy Spirit.

quotation.summary: Augustine reads Matthew 3:16 (the Spirit descending like a dove at Christ's baptism) as prefiguring Christ's body, the Church, in which the baptised receive the Holy Spirit.

explanation: Augustine is showing that the Holy Spirit was given when Jesus breathed on the disciples and again at Pentecost. He insists Christ was not then anointed with the Spirit at His baptism, since He was already the Anointed; rather the dove at the baptism prefigured His body, the Church, in which the baptised receive the Holy Spirit.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads the dove of Matthew 3:16 as prefiguring the Church receiving the Spirit in baptism. (A) The text states that the Spirit of God descended like a dove and alighted on Jesus; it does not state that the dove prefigures the Church. (B) The prefiguration of the Church is Augustine's reading. (D) The doctrine of the Spirit's gift in baptism is a later theological development, not the Gospel's own claim.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book XV, chapter 26, where Augustine treats the giving of the Holy Spirit at Christ's breathing on the disciples and at Pentecost.

Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether 'I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost' is a suitable form of Baptism. The form is Christ's command in Matthew 28:19. In reply to the objection that three personal names should take the plural 'names', Aquinas argues that although there are three personal names of the three persons, there is but one essential name, and the divine power working in Baptism pertains to the essence; therefore the singular 'in the name' is correct. The singular 'name' shared by the three is, for Aquinas, the grammatical sign of the unity of essence.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Tertia Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1272-1273 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article treats the sacramental form of Baptism; Aquinas also argues in q. 66, a. 6 that Christ commanded Baptism to be given with the invocation of the Trinity, and that at Christ's own baptism the Trinity was present in sensible signs (Father in the voice, Son in the human nature, Holy Ghost in the dove).
notes: The quotation is Aquinas's reply to Objection 6 of III, q. 66, a. 5; the baptismal formula itself is Matthew 28:19, which Aquinas cites in the same question (a. 2, obj. 2) as Christ's mandate after His Passion and Resurrection.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae III, q. 66, a. 5, reply to Objection 6
quotation.summary: Aquinas argues that the baptismal form rightly says 'in the name' (singular), not 'in the names', because although there are three personal names, there is but one essential name, and the divine power in Baptism pertains to the essence.
quotation.text: Although there are three personal names of the three Persons, there is but one essential name. Now the Divine power which works in Baptism, pertains to the Essence; and therefore we say, "in the name," and not, "in the names."
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 as naming three persons under one name, and takes the singular 'name' as the sign of one essence. (A) The text commands baptism 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit'; it does not state that the three are one essence or use the language of 'essential name'. (B) The step from the singular 'name' to unity of essence is an inference, which Aquinas presents as a grammatical argument about the form. (D) The essence/person distinction in this form is Aquinas's scholastic formulation and must not be presented as the wording of Matthew 28:19.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 43, a. 7, sed contra, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1043.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether it is fitting for the Holy Ghost to be sent visibly. He answers yes, citing Matthew 3:16: at the Lord's baptism the Holy Ghost descended upon Him in the shape of a dove. The visible mission of the Spirit, for Aquinas, manifests the invisible mission: the Son is sent visibly as the author of sanctification, the Holy Ghost as the sign of sanctification. In his reply to the objections he adds that the Father's voice spoke at the baptism, 'This is My beloved Son' (Matthew 3:17).
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article belongs to q. 43 on the mission of the divine persons, which links the eternal processions to the temporal missions (sending) of Son and Spirit.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 43, a. 7, sed contra
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites Matthew 3:16 (the Holy Ghost descending on the baptised Lord in the shape of a dove) as the authority that the Holy Ghost is fittingly sent visibly.
quotation.text: It is said (Matthew 3:16) that, when our Lord was baptized, the Holy Ghost descended upon Him in the shape of a dove.
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads Matthew 3:16 as the visible mission of the Holy Ghost: the Spirit descends on the Son at His baptism as the sign of sanctification. (A) The text states that the Spirit of God descended like a dove and rested on Jesus, with the Father's voice speaking; it does not use the scholastic vocabulary of 'visible mission' or 'procession'. (D) The visible/invisible mission framework is Aquinas's scholastic formulation, linking the eternal processions to temporal sending, and must not be presented as the wording of Matthew 3:16.

quotation.text: And there cannot be a doubt that our Saviour wished to testify, by a solemn rehearsal, that the perfect light of faith is now exhibited, when he said, 'Go and teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,' since this is the same thing as to be baptised into the name of the one God, who has been fully manifested in the Father, the Son, and the Spirit.
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 16
quotation.summary: Calvin reads the baptismal formula as a solemn rehearsal of the one God now fully manifested in Father, Son, and Spirit, and baptism in the one name as baptism into the one God.

explanation: Calvin argues that the baptismal formula teaches the unity of God and the three persons together: to be baptised 'in the name' of the three is the same as to be baptised into the name of the one God, because that God has been fully manifested in the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. The single name is, for Calvin, the decisive point: it shows that the three named are one God, not three gods.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Matthew 28:19 as teaching both the unity of God (one name) and the three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). (A) The text gives one name in which the three are named. (B) The inference from the single name to one divine essence is Calvin's, drawn from the grammar of the formula. (D) 'Manifested in the Father, the Son, and the Spirit' is Calvin's phrasing of the doctrine, not the text's.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.16, final edition 1559. Calvin is arguing for the deity of the Holy Spirit in particular: the Spirit is named with the Father and the Son in the one baptismal name, which, he argues, no creature could share.

alternativeReadings.summary: The Racovian Catechism concedes that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named together in the baptismal formula and are associated in divine things, but denies that the joint naming proves three persons in one essence; see faustus-socrinus-matt-28-19-001.

citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, section 16. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.

quotation.text: I answer generally in respect to them, that they only prove the existence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and that they are associated in divine things; which I not only admit, but also constantly declare, insomuch that I pronounce that person to be no Christian who either does not know or does not believe this. It is evident, nevertheless, that these testimonies do not prove the matter in dispute; namely, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are three persons in the one essence of God.
quotation.edition: Trans. Thomas Rees (London, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680
quotation.location: The Racovian Catechism, Section III, Chapter 1, 'Of the Nature of God', pp. 56-57
quotation.summary: The Catechism concedes that the joint-naming testimonies prove the existence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and their association in divine things, but denies they prove three persons in one essence.

explanation: The Catechism addresses the three testimonies that name Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together - Matthew 28:19, 1 Corinthians 12:4-6, and 1 John 5:7 - and concedes their force up to a point: they prove the existence of the three and that they are associated in divine things, which the Catechism 'not only admits, but also constantly declares', even pronouncing no Christian anyone who does not believe it. But, it argues, they do not prove the matter in dispute, namely that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons in the one essence of God. The distinction between association in divine things and unity of essence is the Catechism's central argument against the Trinitarian reading of these verses.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) The Catechism reads Matthew 28:19 (with 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 and 1 John 5:7) as proving only the existence and association of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, not three persons in one essence. (A) The text names the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in one baptismal name. (B) The inference that joint naming does not prove unity of essence is the Catechism's. (D) 'Three persons in the one essence of God' is the doctrinal formulation under dispute, not the text's wording.
historicalContext: The Racovian Catechism, Section III, Chapter 1, 'Of the Nature of God', pp. 56-57. First published in Polish at Rakow, 1605; the Rees translation (1818) is from the revised Latin edition of 1680.

alternativeReadings.summary: Calvin reads Matthew 28:19 as teaching both the unity of God (one name) and the three persons: baptism into the one name is baptism into the one God, fully manifested in Father, Son, and Spirit; see john-calvin-matt-28-19-001.

Thomas Rees (London, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680. URL: https://archive.org/stream/racoviancatechi00reesgoog/racoviancatechi00reesgoog_djvu.txt. Accessed 2026-11-20.

quotation.text: It was under this similitude that the Holy Ghost descended from the Father on Christ at His baptism, signifying the infinite love of the Father to the Son, Who is the true David, or beloved, as we said before.
quotation.edition: George P. Fisher (ed.), 'An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity' (1903), CCEL electronic edition
quotation.location: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity, section on the Holy Spirit as love (dove similitude), p. 5 of the CCEL PDF
quotation.summary: Edwards reads the dove at Christ's baptism as signifying the Holy Spirit, who is the infinite love of the Father to the Son.

explanation: In his Discourse on the Trinity, Edwards argues that the Holy Spirit is the infinite love of the Father and the Son. The dove that descended on Christ at his baptism is, on this reading, a similitude of the Spirit: the Holy Ghost descended from the Father on Christ at his baptism 'signifying the infinite love of the Father to the Son', who is 'the true David, or beloved'. The baptism scene (Matthew 3:16) is thus read as a visible representation of the Spirit as the bond of love between Father and Son.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Edwards reads Matthew 3:16 as a similitude of the Holy Spirit, who is the infinite love of the Father to the Son. (A) The text says the Spirit of God descended like a dove and lighted upon Jesus at his baptism. (B) The inference that the dove signifies the Spirit as the Father's love to the Son is Edwards's, drawn from his larger argument that the Spirit is the divine love itself. (D) 'The Holy Spirit is the infinite love of the Father and the Son' is Edwards's doctrinal formulation, not the text's wording.
historicalContext: Discourse on the Trinity, begun early 1730, with additions in the mid- or late 1730s; unpublished in Edwards's lifetime and first published 1903. The essay is a private theological exercise, not a published doctrinal statement; it is recorded here as such. Edwards writes in the Reformed tradition, developing an account of the Trinity in which the Son is God's perfect idea or image of himself and the Spirit is the love between Father and Son.
citation: Jonathan Edwards, 'An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity', ed. George P. Fisher (1903); CCEL electronic edition, p. 5. Edition: George P. Fisher (ed.), 'An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity' (1903), CCEL electronic edition. URL: https://www.CCEL.ORG/ccel/e/edwards/trinity/cache/trinity.pdf. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: No attested dissenting reading of Matthew 3:16 was located in the era sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty; this is absence of evidence in this pass, not a claim that no dissenting reading exists.

quotation.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by Him, and without Him was nothing made.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Irenaeus quotes John 1:1-3 as John's own opening: the Word who was with God and was God is the one by whom the one Almighty God made all things.

explanation: Against Cerinthus and the Nicolaitans, who separated the Creator from the Father of the Lord, Irenaeus argues that John begins his Gospel by teaching one Almighty God who made all things by his Word, and that the Word also bestowed salvation on men included in the creation.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Irenaeus reads John 1:1 as establishing that the Creator and the Father of Jesus Christ are one God, acting by his Word. The verse itself (row A) identifies the Word as God and as the agent of creation; the anti-Gnostic application is Irenaeus's, and the passage is not presented as a later creedal statement (row D).
historicalContext: Against Heresies, written c. 175-185 (range), is Irenaeus's refutation of Valentinian Gnosticism. Book III argues from Scripture that the Creator is the one true God and Father of Jesus Christ; Book IV argues that the one God formed all things by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit.
citation: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, III.11.1, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103311.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: But the Son of God is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; for after the pattern of Him and by Him were all things made, the Father and the Son being one. And, the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, in oneness and power of spirit, the understanding and reason ... of the Father is the Son of God.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.location: A Plea for the Christians, ch. 10
quotation.summary: Athenagoras defends Christians against the charge of atheism: they acknowledge one God, and also a Son of God who is the Father's Logos, 'the Father and the Son being one,' the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son.

explanation: In Plea 10 Athenagoras argues the Son is the Logos of the Father, in idea and in operation; all things were made after his pattern and by him. He also describes the Holy Spirit as an effluence of God, and concludes that Christians who speak of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, declaring 'their power in union and their distinction in order,' should not be called atheists.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Athenagoras's 'the Father and the Son being one' and 'the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son' echo the oneness of John 10:30 ('I and the Father are one'), though he does not quote the verse here; the link is a doctrinal connection drawn by the researcher (row B). His language - the Son as 'the first product of the Father, not as having been brought into existence' - is his own philosophical account, not the later Nicene formulation (row D).
historicalContext: A Plea for the Christians, written c. 176-177 (range), is a petition to the Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus defending Christians against charges of atheism, cannibalism, and immorality. Chapter 10 states the Christian doctrine of God against the charge of atheism.
citation: Athenagoras, A Plea for the Christians, ch. 10, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.logoslibrary.org/athenagoras/plea/10.html (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: The quotation omits a parenthetical Greek phrase (nous kai logos) after 'understanding and reason', marked with an ellipsis.

quotation.text: one of whom, John, says, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, showing that at first God was alone, and the Word in Him. Then he says, The Word was God; all things came into existence through Him; and apart from Him not one thing came into existence.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Theophilus cites John 1:1-3 to show that before anything came into being, God had the Word in himself as his counsellor, his own mind and thought, and that the Word is God, through whom all things came into existence.

explanation: In II.22 Theophilus explains how the uncontainable Father can be said to 'walk in Paradise': his Word, his power and wisdom, assuming the person of the Father, went to the garden. John is cited as one of the 'spirit-bearing men' who teach that the Word was with God, was God, and made all things.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Theophilus reads John 1:1 as teaching that the Word was eternally in God and is God. Note his phrasing - 'at first God was alone, and the Word in Him' - which later theology would express differently; it is recorded as he wrote it (row D: not Nicene language).
historicalContext: To Autolycus, written c. 180 (approximate), is Theophilus's apology addressed to his pagan friend Autolycus. Book II walks through Genesis 1 day by day with allegorising commentary, and explains how the uncontainable Father can be said to walk in Paradise (ch. 22).
citation: Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, II.22, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02042.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: Theophilus's phrasing 'at first God was alone, and the Word in Him' is recorded as written; see relationshipToDoctrine.

quotation.text: Now if He too is God, according to John, (who says,) “The Word was God,” then you have two Beings—One that commands that the thing be made, and the Other that executes the order and creates.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3 (1885)

explanation: In the same chapter, Tertullian turns from Genesis 1:26 to John 1:1-3: because John says 'the Word was God' and 'through whom all things were made', there are two Beings, one who commands creation and one who executes it. He immediately qualifies this as a distinction of Personality, not of Substance, 'in the way of distinction, not of division'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Tertullian reads John 1:1 as establishing that the Word is God and is distinct from the Father who commands, while sharing one substance. (D) This is pre-Nicene: 'two Beings' distinguished by command and execution reflects Tertullian's economic subordination, not the Nicene confession of one essence (homoousios). The reading supports the Son's deity and distinction, but must not be presented as the Nicene doctrine.
historicalContext: Against Praxeas, c. 207-213 (range), written against the modalist Praxeas. Chapter 12 adduces scriptural quotations 'in proof of the plurality of Persons in the Godhead'.

quotation.text: John, however, with more sublimity and propriety, says in the beginning of his Gospel, when defining God by a special definition to be the Word, “And God was the Word, and this was in the beginning with God.”
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885)

explanation: Origen argues that Wisdom, understood as the beginning of the ways of God, is also to be understood as the Word of God, because she discloses the mysteries of divine wisdom to creation. John, he says, defines God as the Word with more sublimity: 'And God was the Word, and this was in the beginning with God.' Whoever assigns a beginning to the Word or Wisdom, Origen warns, is guilty of impiety against the unbegotten Father, since that would deny the Father had always been Father.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Origen reads John 1:1 as John's definition of God as the Word, eternal with God, and uses it to deny that the Word ever began to be. (D) This eternal generation is Origen's own doctrine; it is pre-Nicene, and Origen elsewhere subordinates the Son to the Father (the Father alone is unbegotten and the source). Origen must not be presented as teaching Nicaea's homoousios.
historicalContext: De Principiis, c. 220-230 (range), Book I, ch. 2, §§2-3. Origen is arguing against the idea that God was ever without his Wisdom or Word.

quotation.text: Moreover, this Word “was in the beginning with God, and God was the Word.”
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)

explanation: Novatian cites John 1:1 alongside John 1:3, 1:10-11 and Colossians 1:16 to argue that the Word who became flesh is God: because all things were made by him, he cannot be merely man, who is subsequent to all things, but is God also, since God is prior to all things. The chapter accumulates scriptural proofs that Christ is both man and God.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Novatian reads John 1:1 as stating that the Word is God and was with God in the beginning, and therefore that Christ is God. (D) Novatian's framework is pre-Nicene and subordinationist in structure: the Son derives his being from the Father, who alone is without origin; Novatian does not teach the Nicene homoousios. His reading supports the Son's deity, not the later formulated doctrine as such.
historicalContext: Treatise Concerning the Trinity, c. 250 (approximate), ch. 13, 'That the Same Truth is Proved from the Sacred Writings of the New Covenant'. Written against Sabellian modalism; the oldest extant treatise devoted specifically to the Trinity.

quotation.text: and if, whereas this word can be true of no man, “I and the Father are one,” Christ alone declared this word out of the consciousness of His divinity; […]
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)

explanation: Novatian lists 'I and the Father are one' among words that can be true of no mere man: only Christ, conscious of his divinity, could declare it. Together with Thomas's confession and Romans 9:5, it is offered as proof that Christ is God. The ellipsis marks the continuation of Novatian's sentence ('and if, finally, the Apostle Thomas...'), which is quoted in novatian-john-20-28-001.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Novatian reads John 10:30 as Christ's own claim to divinity, true of him alone and of no mere man. (A) The verse itself states oneness without specifying whether the oneness is of essence, will, or power; Novatian's inference to divinity is his reading. (D) Novatian does not formulate the oneness as Nicene homoousios; his Son remains derived from the Father.
historicalContext: Treatise Concerning the Trinity, c. 250 (approximate), ch. 13, arguing against Sabellius that the Son is distinct from the Father yet divine.
citation: Novatian, Treatise Concerning the Trinity, ch. 13. Translated by Robert Ernest Wallis. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886). CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/novatian/treatise/anf05.vi.iii.xiv.html.
notes: No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task. The Sabellian reading Novatian opposes (Father and Son as one Person) is the target of the whole treatise; see the historical context.

quotation.text: Repeating this same thing, He says: “Father, glorify me with that glory wherewith I was with Thee before the world was.”
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)

explanation: Novatian cites Christ's prayer in John 17:5 to show that the Word possessed glory with the Father before the world was, and that the flesh, ascending to where it had descended from, 'receives that glory which in being shown to have had before the foundation of the world, it is most manifestly proved to be God.' The pre-temporal glory is evidence, for Novatian, of Christ's divinity.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Novatian reads John 17:5 as Christ speaking of glory he had with the Father before the world existed, proving his divinity. (B) The step from 'glory before the world' to 'therefore God' is Novatian's inference, labelled as such. (D) The reading predates Nicaea; Novatian's Son is eternal in glory yet derived from the Father.
historicalContext: Treatise Concerning the Trinity, c. 250 (approximate), ch. 13, in the cumulative scriptural proof that Christ is God.
citation: Novatian, Treatise Concerning the Trinity, ch. 13. Translated by Robert Ernest Wallis. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. quotation.text: and if, finally, the Apostle Thomas, instructed in all the proofs and conditions of Christ’s divinity, says in reply to Christ, “My Lord and my God;” […]
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)

explanation: Novatian treats Thomas's address to the risen Christ, 'My Lord and my God', as the instructed apostle's confession of Christ's divinity, standing alongside 'I and the Father are one' and Romans 9:5 in his cumulative proof that Christ is God. The ellipsis marks the continuation of the sentence into the Romans 9:5 citation, quoted in novatian-rom-9-5-001.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Novatian reads John 20:28 as Thomas confessing Christ as Lord and God. (A) The verse records Thomas's address to Jesus; that it states Christ's deity is Novatian's reading of it, shared by later Nicene writers. (D) The reading predates Nicaea and is not itself the Nicene formulation.
historicalContext: Treatise Concerning the Trinity, c. 250 (approximate), ch. 13, in the cumulative scriptural proof that Christ is God.

quotation.text: ‘The Son was not always;’ for, whereas all things were made out of nothing, and all existing creatures and works were made, so the Word of God Himself was ‘made out of nothing,’ and ‘once He was not,’ and ‘He was not before His origination,’ but He as others ‘had an origin of creation.’
quotation.translation: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson (translators of the Athanasius text preserving the fragments)
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
quotation.location: Athanasius, Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse I, ch. 2, §5, quoting Arius, Thalia

explanation: Athanasius quotes the Thalia of Arius to exhibit the Arian doctrine: God was not always Father but became Father; the Son was not always, but was made out of nothing, 'once was not', and had an origin of creation like other creatures; God made him Word and Wisdom and Son in order to form us by means of him. In §6 Athanasius adds that Arius held the Word to be 'not the very God' but God only in name, by participation of grace, 'alien and unlike in all things to the Father's essence'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Arius read John 1:1 against the Nicene reading: the Word 'was in the beginning' means he was made before other things, not that he is eternal and of the Father's essence. His position is the dissenting reading of John 1:1 in this era and is recorded fairly, as RESEARCH-STANDARDS.md §6 requires. (D) The Council of Nicaea (325) anathematised this teaching ('there was a time when the Son of God was not'); the anathema is a later formulation responding to Arius, not a statement of John 1:1 itself. ATTRIBUTION WARNING: the Thalia survives only in fragments quoted by Athanasius, a hostile witness; the wording is Athanasius's quotation of Arius, not a manuscript of Arius himself.
historicalContext: Thalia, c. 318-321 (range), quoted in Athanasius, Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse I, ch. 2, §§5-6 (c. 356-360). Arius, presbyter of Alexandria, was condemned at Nicaea in 325; the controversy continued until 381.

quotation.text: The Word is God from God; for ‘the Word was God,’ and again, ‘Of whom are the Fathers, and of whom Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen’.
quotation.translation: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
quotation.location: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse IV, §1

explanation: Athanasius opens Discourse IV by proving the substantiality of the Word from Scripture: the Word is God from God because John says 'the Word was God', and Paul says Christ is 'God over all' (Romans 9:5). Since Christ is God's Word, Wisdom, Son, and Power, 'but One God is declared in the divine Scriptures': Father and Son are two, yet the Monad of the Godhead is indivisible and inseparable, and the Word is the Father's own Son, 'from Essence Essential and Substantive, and Being from Being'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Athanasius reads John 1:1 as proof that the Word is God from God, of the Father's own essence, eternal and inseparable from him. (D) This is the Nicene position argued after Nicaea (325): the Word is not a creature and 'once was not' is false. Athanasius's 'from the Father's essence' is the substance of the Nicene homoousios, though the word homoousios itself is not used in this passage.
historicalContext: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse IV, §1, c. 356-360 (range; Discourse IV possibly later). Written against the Arians, who held the Son to be a creature made out of nothing.

quotation.text: This the Lord said, viz. ‘I and the Father are One;’ for neither is the Word separated from the Father, nor was or is the Father ever Wordless; […]
quotation.translation: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
quotation.location: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse IV, §2

explanation: Athanasius argues that Father and Son are two, not one person as Sabellius said, because the Father is Father and the Son is Son, 'and they are one, because He is Son of the Essence of the Father by nature, existing as His own Word.' The Lord's words 'I and the Father are One' show the Word is not separated from the Father, and the Father was never Wordless. The ellipsis marks the continuation ('on this account He says, I in the Father and the Father in Me').
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Athanasius reads John 10:30 as the Son's oneness with the Father by nature, as Son of the Father's essence, while remaining distinct from the Father. (D) This is the post-Nicene defence of Nicaea against both Sabellianism (which collapsed Father and Son into one person) and Arianism (which separated them in essence).
historicalContext: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse IV, §2, c. 356-360 (range; Discourse IV possibly later). The section is headed in the edition 'Illustration of John 10:30, drawn from Deuteronomy 4:4'.

quotation.text: It did not disperse its faith among a plurality of deities, for it heard that He is God of God; nor did it fall into the error of attributing a difference of nature to this God of God, for it learned that He is full of grace and truth.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 9 (1899)

explanation: Hilary recounts his own conversion through reading John 1:1-14: his soul learned from the Gospel that the Word was with God and was God, that the Word became flesh, and that his glory was seen as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. From this he learned that the Creator is 'God of God': faith is not dispersed among many deities, nor is a difference of nature attributed to this God of God. In §10 he quotes the whole of John 1:1-14.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Hilary reads John 1:1 as teaching that the Word is God of God, of the same nature as the Father, eternal and uncreated. (D) Hilary writes in exile c. 356-359, after Nicaea, defending the Nicene faith against the Arians, who held the Son to be created; his 'God of God' echoes the Nicene Creed's language without being a quotation of it.
historicalContext: On the Trinity, Book I, §§10-13, c. 356-359 (range), written during Hilary's exile after the Council of Milan (355). Book I is autobiographical, recounting his path from philosophy to faith.

quotation.text: The Word then is not a mere significant impression on the air, borne by the organs of speech; nor is the Spirit of His mouth a vapour, emitted by the organs of respiration; but the Word is He who was with God in the beginning and was God, and the Spirit of the mouth of God is the Spirit of truth which proceeds from the Father.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8

explanation: Discussing creation, Basil distinguishes the Father as original cause, the Son as creative cause, and the Spirit as perfecting cause, and supports this with Psalm 33:6 ('By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all the host of them by the breath of His mouth'). The Word, he says, is not a mere sound but 'He who was with God in the beginning and was God' (John 1:1), and the Spirit of God's mouth is the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (John 15:26).
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Basil reads John 1:1 as identifying the Word as a subsistent person, God with God in the beginning, not a mere utterance; and he joins it to John 15:26 for the Spirit. (D) Basil's three-cause scheme (Father original cause, Son creative cause, Spirit perfecting cause) is his own pre-381 formulation; it is not the Nicene Creed's language, and it must not be read as if it were.
historicalContext: On the Holy Spirit, c. 375 (approximate), ch. 16, §38, on the fellowship of the Spirit with Father and Son in creation.

quotation.text: You are therefore to perceive three, the Lord who gives the order, the Word who creates, and the Spirit who confirms.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8

explanation: Immediately after identifying the Word of John 1:1 and the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (John 15:26), Basil concludes that in creation one is 'to perceive three, the Lord who gives the order, the Word who creates, and the Spirit who confirms', where confirmation is perfecting according to holiness, and 'there is no sanctification without the Spirit'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Basil reads John 15:26 ('the Spirit of truth which proceeds from the Father') as naming the Spirit who confirms and perfects creation, distinct from the Lord who orders and the Word who creates. (B) The inference from the Spirit's procession and perfecting work to his inseparability from Father and Son is Basil's, labelled as such. (D) Basil writes before Constantinople (381), whose creed would take up the same procession language ('who proceedeth from the Father'); Basil's text is a source for that formulation, not a statement of it.
historicalContext: On the Holy Spirit, c. 375 (approximate), ch. 16, §38, on the fellowship of the Spirit with Father and Son in creation.

quotation.text: I will ask the Father, He says, and He will send you another Comforter, even the spirit of Truth.
quotation.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (1894)

explanation: Gregory traces how the Spirit was 'declared by Jesus' by little and little: 'I will ask the Father, He says, and He will send you another Comforter, even the spirit of Truth' (John 14:16). Jesus said this, Gregory explains, 'that He might not seem to be a rival God, or to make His discourses to them by another authority.' The Spirit then came gradually to dwell in the disciples, 'measuring Himself out to them according to their capacity to receive Him'. In §3 Gregory had already called the Spirit 'the Other Comforter' and 'the True Light which lighteneth every man coming into the world', one Light with Father and Son.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Gregory reads John 14:16 as Jesus promising 'another Comforter', the Spirit of Truth, sent by the Father at Jesus' asking; the 'another' marks the Spirit as a distinct person who is nevertheless one God with Father and Son. (D) Gregory is writing in 380, on the eve of Constantinople (381); his oration is a direct source for the council's confession of the Spirit, not yet the creed itself.
historicalContext: Fifth Theological Oration (Oration 31), c. 380 (approximate), §26, delivered at Constantinople during the struggle against the Arians and the Pneumatomachians, who denied the Spirit's deity.

quotation.text: The Holy Ghost, which proceedeth from the Father; Who, inasmuch as He proceedeth from That Source, is no Creature; and inasmuch as He is not Begotten is no Son; and inasmuch as He is between the Unbegotten and the Begotten is God.
quotation.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 7 (1894)

explanation: Answering the dilemma that the Spirit must be either Unbegotten or Begotten, Gregory appeals to the Saviour's own word: 'The Holy Ghost, which proceedeth from the Father' (John 15:26). Procession is the Spirit's distinctive mode: because he proceeds from the Father he is no creature; because he is not begotten he is no Son; and because he stands between the Unbegotten and the Begotten, he is God. 'What then is Procession?' Gregory asks, and answers that it is as unexplainable as the Father's unbegottenness and the Son's generation.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Gregory reads John 15:26 as giving the Spirit's distinctive property, procession from the Father, which marks him as God, neither creature nor Son. (D) This procession language is the direct source of the Constantinopolitan Creed's 'who proceedeth from the Father' (381); Gregory's oration (380) precedes the council and is not itself the creed.
historicalContext: Fifth Theological Oration (Oration 31), c. 380 (approximate), §8, delivered at Constantinople against those who denied the Spirit's deity (the Pneumatomachians/Macedonians).
