quotation.text: For it is plain that we are to take the Word of God to be the only Son of God, of whom it is afterwards said, And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, on account of that birth of His incarnation, which was wrought in time of the Virgin. But herein is declared, not only that He is God, but also that He is of the same substance with the Father.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine reads John 1:1 ('In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God') as declaring that the Word is the only Son of God, is God, and is of the same substance with the Father.

explanation: Augustine cites John 1:1 against those who said Christ is not God, or not very God, or not the one and only God with the Father. He takes 'the Word' to be the only Son of God, and argues from 'all things were made by Him, and without Him was not anything made' that the Son was not made, and therefore is not a creature but is of the same substance with the Father.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads John 1:1 as declaring the Word to be God and of the same substance with the Father. (A) The text states that the Word was with God and was God, and that all things were made through Him; the technical term 'same substance' (homoousios) is Augustine's, not the Gospel's wording. (B) The step from 'was not made' to 'of the same substance' is Augustine's inference. (D) The consubstantiality formula was fixed at Nicaea (325), before Augustine, and is a formulation about the text, not the text's own vocabulary.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book I, chapter 6, where Augustine collects scriptural testimonies that the Son is very God, of the same substance with the Father.

quotation.text: Some things, then, are so put in the Scriptures concerning the Father and the Son, as to intimate the unity and equality of their substance; as, for instance, I and the Father are one.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine cites John 10:30 ('I and the Father are one') as a text that intimates the unity and equality of the substance of Father and Son.

explanation: Augustine sets out his rule for reading scriptural language about the Son: some texts intimate the unity and equality of substance, some speak of the Son as less according to the form of a servant, and some only intimate that He is of the Father. John 10:30 is his first example of the first class.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads John 10:30 as intimating the unity and equality of the Father's and the Son's substance. (A) The text states 'I and the Father are one'; it does not use the language of substance or essence. (B) The step from 'are one' to 'one substance, equal' is Augustine's inference, governed by his stated rule of reading. (D) The substance vocabulary is a later formulation applied to the text, not the text's own wording.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book II, chapter 1, where Augustine states the double rule for understanding scriptural modes of speech concerning the Son.

quotation.text: And it is proved by many other testimonies of the Divine Word, that the Spirit, who is specially called in the Trinity the Holy Spirit, is of the Father and of the Son: of whom likewise the Son Himself says, Whom I will send unto you from the Father; and in another place, Whom the Father will send in my name.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine argues that the Spirit is of the Father and of the Son, citing John 15:26 ('Whom I will send unto you from the Father') and John 14:26 ('Whom the Father will send in my name').

explanation: In the closing book of De Trinitate, Augustine argues that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son, apart from time. He supports this by joining the two sendings: the Son sends the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26), and the Father sends the Spirit in the Son's name (John 14:26). The two statements are, for Augustine, one sending, showing the Spirit to be of both.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads John 14:26 together with John 15:26 as showing that the Spirit is of the Father and of the Son. (A) John 14:26 states that the Father will send the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, in Christ's name; it does not state eternal procession from the Son. (B) The step from the two sendings to eternal procession from both is Augustine's inference. (D) The double-procession (filioque) formulation is Augustine's own theological development; the East later rejected it, and the difference is recorded, not harmonised (see john-of-damascus-john-15-26-001).
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book XV, chapter 26, the summary and conclusion of the whole work, where Augustine treats the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son.

quotation.text: But when the Comforter has come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth which proceeds from the Father, He shall testify of me? He is said, therefore, not to speak of Himself, in that He proceeds from the Father;
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine argues from John 15:26 that the Spirit is said not to speak of Himself because He proceeds from the Father, and that this does not make Him less than the Father or the Son.

explanation: Augustine is answering the claim that the Spirit must be less because John 16:13 says He shall not speak of Himself. He argues that 'not speaking of Himself' belongs to the Spirit as proceeding from the Father (John 15:26), just as the Son's 'can do nothing of Himself' belongs to Him as being of the Father; in neither case does the language imply inferiority. He also notes that the Spirit 'shall receive of mine' because all things that the Father has are the Son's also.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads John 15:26 as teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, and that His not speaking of Himself marks His procession, not inferiority. (A) The text states that the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father and will testify of Christ. (B) The inference that procession does not imply inferiority is Augustine's argument. (D) The later Western formulation that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son is developed by Augustine elsewhere (De Trinitate XV.26) and must be distinguished from what John 15:26 itself states.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). This passage comes from Book II, chapter 3, where Augustine treats texts about the Holy Spirit that might be taken to imply His inferiority.

quotation.text: For He shall not speak of Himself, but whatsoever He shall hear that shall He speak; and He will show you things to come. He shall glorify me; for He shall receive of mine, and shall show it unto you. […] But because He has rendered the reason why He said, He shall receive of mine (for He says, All things that the Father has are mine; therefore said I, that He shall take of mine); it remains that the Holy Spirit be understood to have of that which is the Father's, as the Son also has.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine argues from John 16:13-15 that the Spirit's receiving from the Son shows the Spirit has of that which is the Father's, as the Son also has, because all things the Father has are the Son's.

explanation: Augustine is answering the claim that John 16:13 ('He shall not speak of Himself') proves the Spirit is less, as if born of Christ as Christ is of the Father. He replies that Christ immediately gives the reason: 'All things that the Father has are mine; therefore said I, that He shall take of mine.' The Spirit is therefore to be understood to have of that which is the Father's, as the Son also has.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads John 16:13-15 as showing that the Spirit has of that which is the Father's, as the Son also has. (A) The text states that the Spirit of truth will guide into all truth, will not speak of Himself, will receive of Christ's and show it, because all things the Father has are Christ's. (B) The conclusion that the Spirit shares the Father's substance equally with the Son is Augustine's inference from the 'all things' clause. (D) The equality-of-substance formulation is later theological language applied to the text.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book II, chapter 3, the same section as augustine-john-15-26-001.

quotation.text: I and the Father are One. By the word 'One' He signifies the Sameness of their Essence: and by the word 'are' He severs into two that which is understood, and again binds them up into One Godhead.
quotation.edition: P. E. Pusey edition/translation (Oxford, 1872), as reproduced at elpenor.org
quotation.summary: Cyril reads John 10:30 as teaching that the Father and the Son are one in sameness of essence, while the word 'are' preserves the distinction of persons, bound up into one Godhead.

explanation: Cyril comments on John 10:29-30, where Christ says 'I and the Father are One'. He argues that 'One' signifies the sameness of the Father's and the Son's essence, while 'are' keeps the two distinct - the Word is not the Father - and yet binds them into one Godhead. The verse is used against the Arians to show that the Son is not a creature but is one in essence with the Father.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Cyril reads John 10:30 as teaching the sameness of the Father's and the Son's essence while preserving two persons. (A) The text states 'I and the Father are one'; it does not use the language of essence (ousia) or Godhead. (B) The step from 'are one' to 'sameness of essence' is Cyril's inference, governed by his argument against Arianism. (D) The essence vocabulary is a later formulation applied to the text.
historicalContext: The Commentary on the Gospel according to John was written 425-428 (range), before the outbreak of the Nestorian controversy. Cyril argues throughout against Arian and Eunomian teaching about the Son and the Holy Spirit.
citation: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on the Gospel according to John, trans. P. E. Pusey, 3 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1872), on John 10:29-30. https://www.elpenor.org/cyril-alexandria/john-commentary-4.asp?pg=62
notes: No book number is asserted for this passage: the commentary survives in parts on elpenor.org, and Books VII and VIII are lost. The quotation is located by the Gospel passage (John 10:29-30) and the elpenor part/page.

quotation.text: And so under the first head is shown what unholy views they hold about the Divine Trinity: they affirm that the person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost is one and the same, as if the same God were named now Father, now Son, and now Holy Ghost: and as if He who begot were not one, He who was begotten, another, and He who proceeded from both, yet another; but an undivided unity must be understood, spoken of under three names, indeed, but not consisting of three persons.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 12, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace, trans. Charles Lett Feltoe (1895)
quotation.summary: Leo I summarises the Priscillianist error he is refuting: that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same person under three names, as if He who begot, He who was begotten, and He who proceeded from both were not distinct persons.

explanation: Leo is writing to Turribius, bishop of Asturia, to refute the Priscillianists. In chapter II he first sets out their error about the Trinity: they teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, the same God named now Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit, an undivided unity under three names but not consisting of three persons. Leo then answers that this is contrary to the Catholic faith, which acknowledges the Trinity of the Godhead to be of one essence, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit indivisible without confusion, eternal without time, equal without difference. The quotation is Leo's summary of the error, not his own doctrine; his own doctrine follows it. The phrase 'He who proceeded from both' occurs only inside Leo's summary of the Priscillianist error he is refuting; his own positive statement says only that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct persons of one essence, indivisible, eternal, and equal, and makes no claim about the Spirit's procession. John 15:26 is not cited in chapter II.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Leo's Letter 15 records the Western understanding of three distinct persons of one essence in the Trinity, against the Priscillianist claim that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same person under three names. The phrase 'He who proceeded from both' occurs only in Leo's summary of the error, not in his own doctrine. (A) John 15:26 states that the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father; it does not state that He proceeds from the Son. (B) The step from the Spirit's procession to procession 'from both' is the Western reading of Leo and Augustine, not the text's claim. (D) The double-procession formulation is a later development; the East rejected it, and the difference is recorded, not harmonised.
historicalContext: Letter 15 was written 21 July 447 (exact, dated in the letter itself) to Turribius, bishop of Asturia, refuting Priscillianist errors in Spain, including the Priscillianist (Sabellian) denial of three distinct persons in the Trinity.

alternativeReadings.summary: John of Damascus holds that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone ('only the Holy Spirit proceedeth from the Father's essence'), not from the Son, while still calling Him the Spirit of the Son. The East/West difference on the Spirit's procession is recorded here, not harmonised.
alternativeReadings.citation: John of Damascus, An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book I, ch. 8 (NPNF Series II, Vol. 9).

citation: Leo the Great, Letter 15, ch. II, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 12, trans. Charles Lett Feltoe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1895). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3604015.htm
notes: CAUTION: the quotation is Leo's summary of the Priscillianist error he is refuting, not his own statement of doctrine. His positive statement follows it: 'Which without doubt is contrary to the Catholic faith, which acknowledges the Trinity of the Godhead to be of one essence in such a way that it believes the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost indivisible without confusion, eternal without time, equal without difference: because it is not the same person but the same essence which fills the Unity in Trinity.'

quotation.text: And only the Holy Spirit proceedeth from the Father's essence, not having been generated but simply proceeding. For this is the doctrine of Holy Scripture.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 9, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace (1898)
quotation.summary: John of Damascus states that only the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father's essence, not by generation but by simple procession, and claims this as the doctrine of Holy Scripture, citing John 15:26.

explanation: John of Damascus states the Eastern doctrine of the Spirit's procession: the Father alone is uncaused; the Son is begotten of the Father; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father's essence, not by generation but by simple procession. He presents this as the doctrine of Holy Scripture, appealing to John 15:26 ('the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father'). In the same chapter he says: 'we speak likewise of the Holy Spirit as from the Father, and call Him the Spirit of the Father. And we do not speak of the Spirit as from the Son.'
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) John of Damascus reads John 15:26 as teaching that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, by simple procession, not by generation. (A) The text states that the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father; it does not state the technical distinction between generation and procession, nor the word 'alone'. (B) The inference that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone is John's, argued from the verse together with his account of the Father as the sole cause. (D) The generation/procession distinction and the rejection of the filioque are later formulations and are recorded here as John's doctrine, not as the Gospel's own claim.
historicalContext: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith was written c. 730-743 (range; exact date not established). Book I, ch. 8 ('Concerning the Holy Trinity') is a compendium of earlier Greek Fathers' teaching on the Trinity, and sets out the Eastern doctrine of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father alone.

alternativeReadings.summary: Augustine holds that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son (De Trinitate XV.26.46; II.3.5). Leo I likewise speaks of the Spirit as proceeding 'from both' (Letter 15, ch. II). The East/West difference is recorded, not harmonised.

Anselm of Canterbury, Monologion, ch. 33, trans. Sidney Norton Deane (Chicago: Open Court, 1903), Logos Virtual Library, https://logoslibrary.org/anselm/monologion/33.html (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Saint Anselm, Proslogium; Monologium; An Appendix in Behalf of the Fool by Gaunilon; and Cur Deus Homo, trans. Sidney Norton Deane (Chicago: Open Court Publishing Co., 1903).
explanation: In Monologion ch. 33 Anselm asks how the supreme Wisdom expresses itself. He argues by analogy with the human mind, which in conceiving itself has with itself its image, its word, born of itself: so the supreme Wisdom, conceiving of itself by expressing itself, begets a likeness of itself consubstantial with it, namely, its Word. The Word is therefore the self-expression of the supreme Wisdom, one in substance with it, and the same Word by which the Creator expresses all He creates. The 'Word' here is the Johannine Word of John 1:1-3, through whom all things were made (developed in chs. 29-31); Anselm does not cite John 1:1 by chapter and verse in ch. 33, and the passage link is recorded as partially verified for that reason.
historicalContext: Written at the abbey of Bec, Normandy, 1075-1076 (certainty: range; completed 1076). The Monologion is Anselm's first major work, an attempt to show by reason alone, without appealing to scriptural authority, what God is like; its account of the Word as the self-expression of the supreme Wisdom became the starting point for later scholastic Trinitarian thought, including Aquinas's treatment of the Word in Summa Theologiae I, q. 34.
notes: PASSAGE LINK PARTIALLY VERIFIED: Anselm does not cite John 1:1 by reference in Monologion ch. 33. The link rests on Anselm's subject — the Word through which all things were created (chs. 29-31) — which is the Word of John 1:1-3. The quotation itself is verified verbatim from the Deane translation.

quotation.edition: English translation by Sidney Norton Deane (Chicago: Open Court, 1903), Logos Virtual Library
quotation.summary: Anselm argues that the supreme Wisdom, conceiving of itself by expressing itself, begets a likeness of itself consubstantial with it, namely, its Word.
quotation.text: Who, then, can deny that the supreme Wisdom, when it conceives of itself by expressing itself, begets a likeness of itself consubstantial with it, namely, its Word?

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Anselm reads the Word — the Word of John 1:1, through whom all things were made — as the supreme Wisdom's self-expression, begotten as a likeness consubstantial with the Wisdom itself. (A) John 1:1 states that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; it does not describe the Word as the Wisdom's self-conception or use the term 'consubstantial'. (B) The analogy from the human mind conceiving itself to the supreme Wisdom begetting its Word is Anselm's reasoning, offered explicitly as rational argument rather than as scriptural authority. (D) 'Consubstantial' as applied to the Word is Nicene vocabulary (homoousios), later than John's Gospel, and must not be presented as John's wording.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 34, a. 1, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1034.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether 'Word' in God is a personal name. He answers that 'Word', taken strictly, signifies the concept of the intellect proceeding from the knower, and therefore signifies something proceeding from another, which is the mark of a personal term in God, since the divine persons are distinguished by origin. The Word of John 1:1 is thus, for Aquinas, the proper name of the Son: the Son alone is properly called Word in God (developed in q. 34, a. 2).
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). Aquinas is working in the scholastic Trinitarian treatise (qq. 27-43), building on Augustine's De Trinitate and Anselm's Monologion, and answering the Arian claim that the Son differs in substance from the Father.
notes: The quotation is Aquinas's own respondeo wording; the Augustinian citation inside the same article is not reproduced here.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 34, a. 1, respondeo
quotation.summary: Aquinas argues that 'Word' in God, taken strictly, signifies the concept of the intellect proceeding from another, and is therefore a personal term, the proper name of the Son.
quotation.text: "Word," according as we use the term strictly of God, signifies something proceeding from another; which belongs to the nature of personal terms in God, inasmuch as the divine persons are distinguished by origin.
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads John 1:1 ('In the beginning was the Word') as naming the Son: the Word is the divine person's proper name, proceeding from the Father by an intelligible emanation. (A) The text of John 1:1 itself states that the Word was with God and was God; it does not use the later scholastic vocabulary of 'personal term' or 'procession by way of intellect'. (D) The formulation of Word as a personal term distinct by relation of origin is Aquinas's thirteenth-century scholastic formulation and must not be projected back onto John's wording.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 39, a. 2, ad 2, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1039.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas is defending the formula that the three persons are 'of one essence' against the objection that Holy Writ never says so in so many words. He replies that, although the phrase is not found verbatim, it is found 'as regards the meaning', and he gives John 10:30 ('I and the Father are one') and John 10:38 ('I am in the Father, and the Father in Me') as the scriptural evidence for that meaning. For Aquinas, 'I and the Father are one' states the unity of essence of Father and Son.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article treats the persons in relation to the essence, defending the Nicene homoousion ('of one essence') against Arian readings.
notes: Aquinas cites John 10:38 alongside John 10:30; John 10:38 is not in the 60-passage inventory, so only John 10:30 is recorded here.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 39, a. 2, reply to Objection 2
quotation.summary: Aquinas says the claim that the three persons are of one essence, though not stated in so many words in Scripture, is stated as regards its meaning, e.g. in John 10:30.
quotation.text: Although we may not find it declared in Holy Writ in so many words that the three persons are of one essence, nevertheless we find it so stated as regards the meaning; for instance, "I and the Father are one (John 10:30)," and "I am in the Father, and the Father in Me (John 10:38)"; and there are many other texts of the same import.
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads John 10:30 as stating, as regards its meaning, that Father and Son are of one essence. (A) The text states 'I and the Father are one'; it does not use the words 'one essence' or the Nicene term homoousion. (B) The step from 'are one' to 'of one essence' is an inference, which Aquinas himself labels as a matter of meaning rather than of wording. (D) The formula 'of one essence' is the later Nicene/scholastic formulation and must not be presented as the wording of John 10:30.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 27, a. 3, sed contra, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1027.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether there is any other procession in God besides the generation of the Word. He answers yes, citing two Johannine texts together: the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Father (John 15:26) and is distinct from the Son, because Christ promises 'another Paraclete' (John 14:16). The word 'another' is the evidence that the Spirit is a distinct person from the Son, and therefore that there is a second procession, the procession of love.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article establishes the two processions (Word by intellect, Love by will) on which the whole scholastic account of the three persons rests.
notes: The same sed contra sentence also cites John 15:26; that citation is recorded separately as thomas-aquinas-john-15-26-001.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 27, a. 3, sed contra
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites John 14:16 ('another Paraclete') together with John 15:26 as evidence that the Holy Ghost is distinct from the Son, so there is a second procession in God besides generation.
quotation.text: The Holy Ghost proceeds from the Father (John 15:26); and He is distinct from the Son, according to the words, "I will ask My Father, and He will give you another Paraclete" (John 14:16).
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads John 14:16 as showing that the Holy Ghost is distinct from the Son ('another Paraclete'), which grounds his claim of a second procession in God, the procession of love. (A) The text promises another Helper/Paraclete; it does not state that the Spirit proceeds by way of the will or that there are two processions. (D) The two-processions framework (Word by intellect, Love by will) is Aquinas's scholastic formulation and must not be presented as the wording of John 14:16.

alternativeReadings.citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 36, a. 2, obj. 3, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1036.htm (accessed 2026-11-20): 'Damascene says (De Fide Orth. i): "We say that the Holy Ghost is from the Father, and we name Him the spirit of the Father; but we do not say that the Holy Ghost is from the Son, yet we name Him the Spirit of the Son."'
alternativeReadings.summary: John of Damascus, as reported by Aquinas, says the Holy Ghost is from the Father and is named the Spirit of the Father, but is not said to be from the Son, although He is named the Spirit of the Son. Aquinas records this Eastern position in the objection and then argues against it in the respondeo, holding that the Holy Ghost is from the Son. The disagreement is therefore recorded here as attested, not harmonised.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 36, a. 2, obj. 1, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1036.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: In q. 36, a. 2, Aquinas asks whether the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Son. The opening objection states the Eastern case: Scripture says only that the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Father, 'as appears from John 15:26: "The Spirit of truth, Who proceeds from the Father."' Aquinas answers in the respondeo that the Holy Ghost must be from the Son, because otherwise the Son and the Holy Ghost could not be personally distinguished, since the divine persons are distinguished only by opposite relations. The quotation records the Johannine text as Aquinas himself presents it in this article; the reading he defends is the filioque, and the Eastern objection is recorded in alternativeReadings.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article is the central scholastic treatment of the filioque, written in the aftermath of the 1054 schism and the long East-West dispute over the Spirit's procession; Aquinas also cites the Council of Constantinople's creed and Damascene in the objections.
notes: The quotation is from the article's Objection 1, i.e. the position Aquinas is about to answer; it is Aquinas's own text presenting the Johannine wording, and the record distinguishes the objection's citation from Aquinas's defended conclusion in the respondeo.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 36, a. 2, Objection 1
quotation.summary: Aquinas presents the objection that Scripture says the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Father, as appears from John 15:26, and does not say He proceeds from the Son; he then argues in the respondeo that the Holy Ghost is from the Son.
quotation.text: But in the Sacred Scripture we are not told that the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Son; but only that He proceeds from the Father, as appears from John 15:26: "The Spirit of truth, Who proceeds from the Father."
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas treats John 15:26 as the text stating that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, and argues (in the respondeo of the same article) that the Spirit must also be from the Son if Son and Spirit are to be personally distinct. (A) The text states that the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father; it does not state that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. (B) The step from 'proceeds from the Father' to 'proceeds from the Father and the Son' is Aquinas's inference from the principle that persons are distinguished only by opposite relations. (D) The filioque formulation is a later Western formulation; the East-West disagreement over it is recorded in alternativeReadings and must not be harmonised away.

quotation.text: Very differently does the Evangelist teach in this passage; for he does not ascribe to the Speech a beginning of time, but says that he was from the beginning, and thus rises beyond all ages.
quotation.edition: Calvin's Commentaries, Vol. 34: John, Part I; tr. John King, 1847-50
quotation.location: Commentary on the Gospel According to John, ch. 1, on John 1:1 (Vol. 34)
quotation.summary: Calvin reads 'from the beginning' as excluding any beginning in time for the Word, and therefore as asserting his eternity.

explanation: Calvin reads John's opening as asserting the eternal divinity of Christ: the Word (which Calvin, following his preference for 'Speech', renders 'the Speech') has no beginning in time but 'was from the beginning', rising 'beyond all ages'. The words 'the Speech was with God' both distinguish the Word from the Father and exclude him from the order of created things.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads John 1:1 as asserting Christ's eternal divinity and his distinct subsistence from the Father. (A) The text itself states that the Word was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. (B) The inference that the Word is therefore uncreated and eternal is drawn by Calvin from 'was from the beginning' together with 'was with God'. (D) The later language of 'person' and 'essence' is Calvin's doctrinal vocabulary, not the Evangelist's.
historicalContext: Commentary on John, published 1 January 1553, Geneva; based on lectures in the Congregation from 1550. Calvin writes against Servetus's claim (see alternativeReadings) that the Word began to exist at creation, and against Arian readings of 'beginning'.

alternativeReadings.summary: As reported by Calvin in this same commentary, Servetus held that the eternal Speech began to exist when it was displayed in the creation of the world, as if it did not exist before its power was made known by external operation. Calvin rejects this reading. No verified quotation from Servetus's own writings was obtained in this pass; his position is recorded here only as Calvin reports it.
The Racovian Catechism reads 'the Word' in John 1:1 as the immediate interpreter and executor of the divine will, not as a pre-existent divine person; see faustus-socrinus-john-1-1-001.

citation: John Calvin, Commentary on the Gospel According to John, in Calvin's Commentaries, vol. 34, tr. John King (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1847-50), ch. 1, on John 1:1. Edition: Calvin's Commentaries, Vol. 34: John, Part I; tr. John King, 1847-50. URL: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/chr/calvin/cc34/cc34006.htm. Accessed 2026-11-20.

quotation.text: The ancients made a wrong use of this passage to prove that Christ is (ὁμοούσιος) of the same essence with the Father. For Christ does not argue about the unity of substance, but about the agreement which he has with the Father, so that whatever is done by Christ will be confirmed by the power of his Father.
quotation.edition: Calvin's Commentaries, Vol. 34: John, Part I; tr. John King, 1847-50
quotation.location: Commentary on the Gospel According to John, ch. 10, on John 10:30 (Vol. 34)
quotation.summary: Calvin denies that John 10:30 proves unity of substance; he holds it speaks of the agreement between Christ and the Father in action.

explanation: This is a negative reading, and it is recorded as such. Calvin holds that 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30) refers to the agreement of Christ with the Father in his works, not to unity of substance, and he criticises the ancient (patristic) use of the verse as a proof of the homoousios. Calvin is himself a Trinitarian; his point is about what this particular verse proves, not about the doctrine. The reading is included because it shows Calvin's exegetical restraint: a verse may be true to the doctrine yet not prove it.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads John 10:30 as agreement in action, not as a proof of unity of substance. (A) The text says 'I and my Father are one'. (B) The inference Calvin rejects is that 'one' here means 'one in substance'; the inference he accepts is that the verse shows Christ's works are confirmed by the Father's power. (D) The term homoousios is the fourth-century doctrinal term, not the Evangelist's word.
historicalContext: Commentary on John, published 1 January 1553, Geneva. Calvin's comment reflects his general practice of refusing to make a verse prove more than he thinks it says, even when the doctrine it is made to prove is one he holds.
citation: John Calvin, Commentary on the Gospel According to John, in Calvin's Commentaries, vol. 34, tr. John King (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1847-50), ch. 10, on John 10:30. Edition: Calvin's Commentaries, Vol. 34: John, Part I; tr. John King, 1847-50. URL: https://sacred-texts.com/book/calvin-s-commentaries-part-34-john-part-i/chapter-10. Accessed 2026-11-20.

Calvin's 'ancients' are the patristic writers who used this verse as a proof of the homoousios; that use is described in the explanation above. quotation.text: He calls the Spirit another Comforter, on account of the difference between the blessings which we obtain from both. The peculiar office of Christ was, to appease the wrath of God by atoning for the sins of the world, to redeem men from death, to procure righteousness and life; and the peculiar office of the Spirit is, to make us partakers not only of Christ himself, but of all his blessings.
quotation.edition: Calvin's Commentaries, Vol. 35: John, Part II; tr. John King, 1847-50
quotation.location: Commentary on the Gospel According to John, ch. 14, on John 14:16 (Vol. 35)
quotation.summary: Calvin reads 'another Comforter' as marking a distinction of persons: the Spirit differs from the Son in his peculiar office, so that the Spirit is another than the Son.

explanation: Calvin holds that 'another Comforter' (John 14:16) implies a distinction of persons: there must be some peculiarity in which the Spirit differs from the Son, so as to be another than the Son. The difference lies in their offices: Christ's office is to atone, redeem, and procure righteousness and life; the Spirit's office is to make believers partakers of Christ himself and of all his blessings. In the same section Calvin notes that the Spirit is the gift of the Father obtained by Christ's prayers, and that Christ promises 'I will send Him to you' (John 16:7); as Mediator he obtains the Spirit's grace from the Father, and as God he bestows that grace from himself, so the Spirit is sent by both. John 15:26 is not mentioned in the section.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads John 14:16 as implying a distinction of persons between the Spirit and the Son. (A) The text calls the Spirit 'another Comforter'. (B) The inference from 'another' to a distinct person is Calvin's, drawn from the difference of offices. (D) 'Person' and 'peculiar office' are Calvin's doctrinal vocabulary, not the Evangelist's words.
historicalContext: Commentary on John, published 1 January 1553, Geneva. The comment belongs to Calvin's farewell-discourse exposition, where he treats the Spirit's distinct mission after Christ's departure.
citation: John Calvin, Commentary on the Gospel According to John, in Calvin's Commentaries, vol. 35, tr. John King (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1847-50), ch. 14, on John 14:16. quotation.text: We, therefore, again conclude, that the Word was eternally begotten by God, and dwelt with him from everlasting.
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 8
quotation.summary: Calvin concludes from John 17:5 that the Word was eternally begotten and dwelt with the Father from everlasting.

explanation: Commenting on Christ's prayer 'glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was' (John 17:5), Calvin concludes that the Word was eternally begotten by God and dwelt with him from everlasting. The glory Christ had before the world was, on this reading, is not a glory merely decreed in God's purpose but one actually possessed before creation, which proves the Son's eternal subsistence with the Father.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads John 17:5 as asserting the Son's eternal begetting and eternal dwelling with the Father. (A) The text says Christ had glory with the Father before the world was. (B) The inference from pre-world glory to eternal begetting is Calvin's. (D) 'Eternally begotten' is later doctrinal language (eternal generation), not the Evangelist's wording.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.8, final edition 1559. Calvin is arguing against those who made the Word begin at creation or at the incarnation; the pre-world glory of John 17:5 is his evidence that the Son subsisted with the Father from everlasting.

alternativeReadings.summary: The Racovian Catechism reads John 17:5 as a request that Christ be given in actual possession the glory he had with God only in God's purposes and decrees before the world was; see faustus-socrinus-john-17-5-001.

citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, section 8. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.

quotation.text: But Jesus is called the Word or Speech of God because he is the immediate interpreter, and at the same time the executor, of the divine will: for this properly belongs to the Word of God.
quotation.edition: Trans. Thomas Rees (London, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680
quotation.location: The Racovian Catechism, Section IV, Chapter 1, 'Of the Person of Christ', p. 140
quotation.summary: The Catechism holds that Jesus is called the Word because he is the immediate interpreter and executor of God's will, not because he is a pre-existent divine person.

explanation: The Catechism denies that 'the Word' in John 1:1 proves a divine nature in Christ. Jesus is called the Word or Speech of God, it says, because he is the immediate interpreter and executor of the divine will, 'for this properly belongs to the Word of God'. It adds that it cannot be proved from Christ's being the Word of God that he possesses a divine nature, and that 'the contrary is the rather to be inferred; for since he is the word of the one God, it is evident that he is not that one God.' The reading is attributed here to the Socinian tradition of the Catechism, not to Socinus as sole author; see the work record.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) The Catechism reads John 1:1 as naming Christ the Word because he interprets and executes God's will, and denies that the verse proves his divine nature. (A) The text says the Word was in the beginning, was with God, and was God. (B) The inference that 'word of the one God' excludes being that one God is the Catechism's. (D) The debate over 'person' and 'nature' is the later doctrinal framework in which the Catechism argues.
historicalContext: The Racovian Catechism, Section IV, Chapter 1, 'Of the Person of Christ'. First published in Polish at Rakow, 1605; the Rees translation (1818) is from the revised Latin edition of 1680. The Catechism is the doctrinal statement of the Polish Brethren, written after Socinus's death in 1604 by Smalcius, Moskorzowski, and Volkel.

alternativeReadings.summary: Calvin reads John 1:1 as asserting the eternal divinity of Christ: the Word has no beginning in time but 'was from the beginning'; see john-calvin-john-1-1-001.

citation: The Racovian Catechism, trans. Thomas Rees (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, 1818), Section IV, Chapter 1, p. 140. Edition: Trans. Thomas Rees (London, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680. URL: https://archive.org/stream/racoviancatechi00reesgoog/racoviancatechi00reesgoog_djvu.txt. Accessed 2026-11-20.

quotation.text: But the meaning of the passage is, that Christ beseeches God to give him in actual possession, with himself, the glory which he had with him, in his purposes and decrees, before the world was.
quotation.edition: Trans. Thomas Rees (London, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680
quotation.location: The Racovian Catechism, Section IV, Chapter 1, 'Of the Person of Christ', p. 144
quotation.summary: The Catechism reads John 17:5 as a request for the glory Christ had with God only in God's purposes and decrees before the world, not in actual pre-existent possession.

explanation: The Catechism argues that John 17:5 does not prove Christ's pre-existence. Christ, it says, beseeches God to give him in actual possession the glory which he had with him 'in his purposes and decrees' before the world was - that is, the glory was his only in God's foreordained purpose, not in an actual pre-world existence. The distinction between actual possession and possession in God's decree is the Catechism's central move against the orthodox reading of the verse.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) The Catechism reads John 17:5 as a request for glory held only in God's purposes and decrees before the world, and therefore denies that the verse proves pre-existence. (A) The text says Christ had glory with the Father before the world was. (B) The inference that this glory was held only in God's decree is the Catechism's. (D) The framework of 'purposes and decrees' is the Catechism's theological vocabulary, not the Evangelist's wording.
historicalContext: The Racovian Catechism, Section IV, Chapter 1, 'Of the Person of Christ', pp. 142-144. First published in Polish at Rakow, 1605; the Rees translation (1818) is from the revised Latin edition of 1680.

quotation.text: Peter’s words to Sapphira, How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? You have not lied unto men, but unto God, show that sins against the Holy Spirit and against God are the same; […]
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8

explanation: Basil argues that the Holy Spirit is inseparable from the Father and the Son in every operation. Peter's words to Sapphira (Acts 5:3-4, 9) show that lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God, so 'sins against the Holy Spirit and against God are the same'. The ellipsis marks the continuation ('and thus you might learn that in every operation the Spirit is closely conjoined with, and inseparable from, the Father and the Son').
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Basil reads Acts 5:3-4 as identifying the Holy Spirit with God: to lie to the Spirit is to lie to God. (B) The step from 'lying to the Spirit is lying to God' to 'the Spirit is God, of the same nature as the Father' is Basil's inference, labelled as such. (D) Basil is writing after Nicaea and before Constantinople (381); he argues for the Spirit's inseparability but does not in this treatise call the Spirit homoousios.
historicalContext: On the Holy Spirit, c. 375 (approximate), ch. 16, §37, addressed to Amphilochius of Iconium against the Pneumatomachians ('Spirit-fighters'), who held the Spirit to be a creature.
citation: Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit. Translated by Blomfield Jackson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace. New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3203.htm.
notes: The Pneumatomachian reading (the Spirit as a creature, not God) is the position Basil is refuting in this chapter; no Pneumatomachian reading of Acts 5:3 specifically was verified in the sources checked. No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task.

quotation.text: Peter, when he rebuked Ananias for having lied to the Holy Spirit, said, that he had not lied unto men, but unto God.
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 15
quotation.summary: Calvin reads Peter's words to Ananias as equating lying to the Holy Spirit with lying to God, and therefore as proof of the Spirit's deity.

explanation: Calvin cites Acts 5:3-4 as the decisive proof of the Spirit's deity: Peter says Ananias has lied to the Holy Spirit, and then explains that he has not lied to men but to God. To lie to the Spirit is, on Calvin's reading, to lie to God, because the Spirit is God. The passage is used in Institutes I.xiii.15 as the conclusion of his Old and New Testament evidence for the Spirit's deity.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Acts 5:3-4 as identifying the Holy Spirit with God. (A) The text says Ananias lied to the Holy Spirit, and then that he lied not to men but to God. (B) The inference that the two statements identify the Spirit with God is Calvin's. (D) 'Deity' and 'person' are later doctrinal terms applied to the text.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.15, final edition 1559. Calvin is concluding his proof of the Spirit's deity; the Acts passage is presented as the clearest New Testament evidence.
citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, section 15. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: No attested dissenting reading of Acts 5:3 was located in the era sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty; this is absence of evidence in this pass, not a claim that no dissenting reading exists.

quotation.text: and if, besides, the Apostle Paul says, “Whose are the fathers, and of whom Christ came according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for evermore,” writing in his epistles; […]
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)

explanation: Novatian cites Paul's words in Romans 9:5, 'who is over all, God blessed for evermore', as apostolic testimony that Christ, who came according to the flesh, is God. It closes his series of New Testament proofs in chapter 13, after which he concludes, 'reasonably Christ is God.' The ellipsis marks the continuation of the sentence.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Novatian reads Romans 9:5 as Paul calling Christ 'God over all'. (A) The verse's punctuation and reference are disputed in modern scholarship (whether 'God blessed for evermore' refers to Christ or is a separate doxology to God the Father); Novatian's reading takes it as referring to Christ, and that attribution to Novatian is what is recorded here. (D) The reading predates Nicaea.
historicalContext: Treatise Concerning the Trinity, c. 250 (approximate), ch. 13, concluding the chapter's proof that Christ is God.
citation: Novatian, Treatise Concerning the Trinity, ch. 13. Translated by Robert Ernest Wallis. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886). CCEL: https://ccel.org/ccel/novatian/treatise/anf05.vi.iii.xiv.html.
notes: The modern dispute over the punctuation and referent of Romans 9:5 is noted in the relationshipToDoctrine field; no modern scholarly source was checked for this note, and it is flagged for the verifier rather than asserted as a verified claim.

quotation.text: And since Christ is God from God, and God’s Word, Wisdom, Son, and Power, therefore but One God is declared in the divine Scriptures. For the Word, being Son of the One God, is referred to Him of whom also He is; so that Father and Son are two, yet the Monad of the Godhead is indivisible and inseparable.
quotation.translation: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
quotation.location: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse IV, §1

explanation: In the same opening section, Athanasius draws the conclusion from John 1:1 and Romans 9:5 together: because Christ is God from God, the Scriptures declare one God, while Father and Son are two and the Monad of the Godhead remains indivisible. Romans 9:5 ('God over all') is one of the two texts on which the argument is built.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Athanasius reads Romans 9:5 as Paul calling Christ 'God over all', and uses it with John 1:1 to argue for one God in Father and Son. (A) As with Novatian's use, the verse's reference is disputed in modern scholarship; Athanasius's reading takes it as referring to Christ, and that attribution is what is recorded here. (D) The argument defends the Nicene settlement after 325.
historicalContext: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse IV, §1, c. 356-360 (range; Discourse IV possibly later).
citation: Athanasius, Four Discourses Against the Arians. Translated by John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892). New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28161.htm (Discourse I); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28162.htm (Discourse II); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28164.htm (Discourse IV).
notes: The modern dispute over the punctuation and referent of Romans 9:5 is noted in the relationshipToDoctrine field; no modern scholarly source was checked for this note, and it is flagged for the verifier rather than asserted as a verified claim. Authorship: Discourse IV is of disputed authorship. The New Catholic Encyclopedia states a fourth Discourse 'is now considered as definitely spurious', and Quasten holds the first three discourses form a single continuous work by Athanasius while the fourth 'was added later by an unknown author' and 'differs in address, content, and style'. This interpretation is of the text as printed under Athanasius's name in NPNF2 vol. 4, not an assertion that Athanasius wrote Discourse IV.

quotation.text: And we do not speak of the Spirit as from the Son: but yet we call Him the Spirit of the Son. For if any one hath not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His, saith the divine apostle.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 9, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace (1898)
quotation.summary: John of Damascus holds that the Spirit is not spoken of as from the Son, yet is called the Spirit of the Son, citing Romans 8:9 ('if any one hath not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His').

explanation: John of Damascus states the Eastern doctrine: the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father's essence, not having been generated but simply proceeding, and is not spoken of as from the Son. Nevertheless He is called the Spirit of the Son, because the apostle says that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him (Romans 8:9). For John, 'Spirit of the Son' describes the Spirit's manifestation through the Son, not His eternal procession from the Son.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) John of Damascus reads Romans 8:9 as warrant for calling the Spirit 'the Spirit of the Son' while denying that the Spirit is from the Son. (A) The text states that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him; it does not state a doctrine of the Spirit's procession. (B) The distinction between 'Spirit of the Son' and 'from the Son' is John's theological construction. (D) The East/West difference on procession is a later formulation and is recorded here, not harmonised (see the alternative reading).
historicalContext: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith was written c. 730-743 (range; exact date not established). Book I, ch. 8 ('Concerning the Holy Trinity') is a compendium of earlier Greek Fathers' teaching on the Trinity, and sets out the Eastern doctrine of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father alone.

alternativeReadings.summary: Augustine holds that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son (De Trinitate XV.26.46; II.3.5). Leo I likewise speaks of the Spirit as proceeding 'from both' (Letter 15, ch. II). The East/West difference is recorded, not harmonised.
alternativeReadings.citation: Augustine, On the Holy Trinity, Book XV, ch. 26 (NPNF Series I, Vol. 3); Leo the Great, Letter 15, ch. II (NPNF Series II, Vol. 12).

citation: John of Damascus, An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book I, ch. 8, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, Vol. 9, trans. S. D. F. Salmond (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1898). https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nicene_and_Post-Nicene_Fathers:_Series_II/Volume_IX/John_of_Damascus/An_Exact_Exposition_of_the_Orthodox_Faith/Book_I/Chapter_8

quotation.text: Why should Paul have feared to place Christ on the Judgment-seat of God, after he had so openly proclaimed his divinity, when he said that he was God over all, blessed for ever?
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 11
quotation.summary: Calvin reads Romans 9:5 as Paul openly proclaiming Christ's divinity by calling him 'God over all, blessed for ever'.

explanation: In Institutes I.xiii.11 Calvin cites Romans 9:5 ('who is over all, God blessed for ever') as a direct ascription of deity to Christ: Paul, he says, had 'so openly proclaimed his divinity' that there was nothing left to fear in placing Christ on the judgment-seat of God. The verse is one of a series of New Testament proofs of the Son's deity in the section, alongside John 20:28, Philippians 2:6, 1 Corinthians 8:6, and 1 John 5:20.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Romans 9:5 as calling Christ 'God over all, blessed for ever', and therefore as a direct proof of his deity. (A) The text applies the words 'God over all, blessed for ever' to Christ. (B) The inference that the ascription proves Christ's deity is Calvin's; the punctuation of the verse (whether 'God over all' is a doxology to the Father or an ascription to Christ) is itself disputed, and Calvin reads it as an ascription to Christ. (D) 'Deity' is later doctrinal vocabulary applied to the text.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.11, final edition 1559. Calvin is gathering New Testament proofs of the Son's deity; Romans 9:5 is presented as the most open of them.
citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, section 11. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: The punctuation of Romans 9:5 is disputed in modern scholarship (ascription to Christ versus a doxology to the Father); Calvin reads it as an ascription to Christ. No attested dissenting reading from the era was located in the sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty.

quotation.text: yet to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we through Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by Him.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Quoting 1 Corinthians 8:4-6, Irenaeus argues that Paul distinguishes the one God the Father, from whom are all things, from idols called gods, and confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things.

explanation: In III.6.5 Irenaeus cites Paul against the Gnostic multiplication of gods: Paul separates 'those which are indeed called gods, but which are none' from the one God the Father, and confesses in the most decided manner one Lord Jesus Christ.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is Irenaeus's use of the passage (row C) against Gnostic aeons: one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ, with all things from the Father through the Son. The passage itself (row A) states one God and one Lord; it does not state the later doctrine of the Trinity (row D), and Irenaeus does not claim that it does.
historicalContext: Against Heresies, written c. 175-185 (range), is Irenaeus's refutation of Valentinian Gnosticism. Book III argues from Scripture that the Creator is the one true God and Father of Jesus Christ; Book IV argues that the one God formed all things by means of the Word and the Holy Spirit.
citation: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, III.6.5, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103306.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: For, it is said, there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and differences of administrations, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which works all in all.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8

explanation: In the same section, Basil quotes 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 (with 12:11) to show the joint operation of Spirit, Lord, and God: God works the differences of operations, the Lord the diversities of administrations, while the Holy Spirit is present too, dispensing the gifts. The apostle names Spirit first, Son second, and God the Father third, which Basil insists does not reverse their rank; the order follows our habits of thought when receiving gifts.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Basil reads 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 as showing the Spirit, the Lord, and God working inseparably together in the distribution of gifts. (B) The inference that inseparable operation implies inseparability of nature is Basil's, labelled as such. (D) Basil is writing between Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381); the passage supports the Spirit's divine rank without stating the later creedal formula.
historicalContext: On the Holy Spirit, c. 375 (approximate), ch. 16, §37, against the Pneumatomachians.
citation: Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit. Translated by Blomfield Jackson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace. New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3203.htm.
notes: No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task.

quotation.text: Who is this one divine Person? The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
quotation.edition: Trans. Thomas Rees (London, 1818), from the revised Latin edition of 1680
quotation.location: The Racovian Catechism, Section III, Chapter 1, 'Of the Nature of God', p. 54
quotation.summary: The Catechism answers its own question - who is the one divine Person? - with the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, proved from 1 Corinthians 8:6.

explanation: In Section III, Chapter 1, 'Of the Nature of God', the Catechism asks who the one divine Person is and answers: 'The Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.' Its proof is 1 Corinthians 8:6, 'To us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things' (together with John 17:3 and Ephesians 4:6). The verse is therefore the Catechism's central proof text for its claim that the one God is the Father alone, and that the Son and the Spirit are not persons in the one divine essence.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) The Catechism reads 1 Corinthians 8:6 as identifying the one God with the Father alone. (A) The text says 'to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things'. (B) The inference that 'one God, the Father' excludes the Son from the divine essence is the Catechism's. (D) 'One divine Person' is the Catechism's doctrinal phrasing, not Paul's wording.
historicalContext: The Racovian Catechism, Section III, Chapter 1, 'Of the Nature of God', p. 54. First published in Polish at Rakow, 1605; the Rees translation (1818) is from the revised Latin edition of 1680.

alternativeReadings.summary: Calvin cites the same verse in Institutes I.xiii.11 ('but to us there is but one God') while affirming the Son's deity: for Calvin the verse proves the unity of God, not that the Father alone is God. No standalone Calvin interpretation of 1 Corinthians 8:6 was written in this pass.
