notes: Attribution: this reading is the Catechism's, associated with the Socinian tradition. See the attribution verification record ver-p5-racovian-catechism-attribution-001.

quotation.text: But both Him, and the Son (who came forth from Him and taught us these things, and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him), and the prophetic Spirit, we worship and adore, knowing them in reason and truth
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Answering the charge of atheism, Justin says Christians worship the true God the Father, the Son who came forth from him, and the prophetic Spirit - naming Father, Son, and Spirit together as objects of worship, alongside the host of good angels in the same sentence.

explanation: In First Apology 6 Justin denies the charge of atheism: Christians are 'atheists' only toward the pagan gods, while they worship the Father, the Son, and the prophetic Spirit. The sentence also names the host of good angels, a feature of Justin's list that later readers have found puzzling; it is reproduced here verbatim and not smoothed over.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Justin names Father, Son, and Spirit together in worship, paralleling the threefold pattern of 2 Corinthians 13:14 (the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit). He does not quote 2 Corinthians 13:14 here; the link is a doctrinal connection drawn by the researcher, labelled as such (row B). Justin's language - including the angels and 'the Son who came forth from Him' - is not the later Nicene formulation (row D).
historicalContext: First Apology, written c. 150-155 (range) and addressed to Emperor Antoninus Pius, defends Christians against charges of atheism and immorality and describes Christian worship, including baptism (ch. 61) and the refutation of atheism (ch. 6).
citation: Justin Martyr, First Apology, ch. 6, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: Justin's sentence also names the host of good angels alongside Father, Son, and Spirit; reproduced verbatim and not smoothed over.

quotation.text: Wherefore also I praise You for all things, I bless You, I glorify You, along with the everlasting and heavenly Jesus Christ, Your beloved Son, with whom, to You, and the Holy Ghost, be glory both now and to all coming ages. Amen.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: The letter from the church of Smyrna reports Polycarp's final prayer at the stake: glory to God the Father, along with Jesus Christ his beloved Son, and the Holy Ghost - the threefold doxology paralleling the grace, love, and fellowship of 2 Corinthians 13:14.

explanation: In Martyrdom of Polycarp 14, bound at the stake, Polycarp thanks God the Father of Jesus Christ for counting him worthy of the martyrs' cup and resurrection through the incorruption of the Holy Spirit, and closes by giving glory to the Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit. The prayer is reported by the letter's authors, the church of Smyrna, not written by Polycarp himself.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): the letter records a threefold doxology - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit receiving glory together - consistent with the threefold pattern of 2 Corinthians 13:14, which the letter does not quote; the link is a doctrinal connection drawn by the researcher (row B). The verse (row A) is Paul's benediction; the prayer is the Smyrnaeans' report of Polycarp's words.
historicalContext: Martyrdom of Polycarp, written c. 155-160 (range), is a letter from the church of Smyrna to the church of Philomelium reporting Polycarp's arrest and burning. Chapter 14 gives Polycarp's prayer at the stake, as reported by the letter's authors; Polycarp is the subject of the letter, not its author.
citation: Church of Smyrna, Martyrdom of Polycarp, ch. 14, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0102.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: The prayer quoted is Polycarp's prayer as reported by the letter's authors, the church of Smyrna; Polycarp is the subject, not the author, of the work.

quotation.text: We read The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost, and again I beseech you for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8

explanation: Defending the doxology 'with the Son together with the Holy Ghost' against those who object to the preposition 'with', Basil argues that Scripture joins the names with 'and' in the same way: 'The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Ghost' (2 Corinthians 13:14, cited as 13:13 in the edition's numbering). The conjunction of the three names shows their conjunction in glory; 'with' sets forth the distinction of the hypostases and the inseparability of the fellowship, and refutes both Sabellius and those who separate the Son from the Father and the Spirit from the Son.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Basil reads 2 Corinthians 13:14 as Scripture joining the names of the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit in one benediction, which warrants joining them in the doxology. (A) The verse itself is a benediction naming the three; it does not state that they are one God or one substance. (D) Basil's argument is about liturgical language (c. 375), not a creedal definition; the later creed of 381 would confess the Spirit as worshipped and glorified with Father and Son.
historicalContext: On the Holy Spirit, c. 375 (approximate), ch. 25, §59, on the use of 'with' in the doxology, against the Pneumatomachians and in answer to critics of Basil's own liturgical language.
citation: Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit. Translated by Blomfield Jackson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 8, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace. New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3203.htm.
notes: Numbering flag: the NPNF2 edition cites this verse as 2 Corinthians 13:13; modern editions number it 13:14. No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task.

quotation.text: Now the Lord is that Spirit; and then, lest any one should think the Son to be signified, and to be called the Spirit on account of His incorporeal substance, has gone on to say, And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty; and no one ever doubted the Spirit of the Lord to be the Holy Spirit.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine reads 2 Corinthians 3:17 ('Now the Lord is that Spirit') as showing that the Holy Spirit is called Lord, so the name 'Lord' belongs to the Spirit as well as to the Father and the Son.

explanation: Augustine is arguing that the name 'Lord' is not appropriated to the Son alone. He cites 2 Corinthians 3:17, 'Now the Lord is that Spirit', and notes that Paul immediately adds 'where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty', so the Spirit meant cannot be the Son but is the Holy Spirit, who is therefore also called Lord.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads 2 Corinthians 3:17 as showing that the Holy Spirit is called Lord. (A) The verse states that the Lord is the Spirit and that where the Spirit of the Lord is there is liberty; it does not name the Trinity or state the doctrine. (B) Identifying 'the Lord' here with the Holy Spirit rather than the Son is Augustine's reading, argued from the following clause. (D) The formulated doctrine is later and is not read back into the verse.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book II, chapter 10, where Augustine asks whether the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, or the Trinity itself appeared to the fathers.
citation: Augustine, On the Holy Trinity (De Trinitate), in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff, trans. Arthur West Haddan (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887), Book 2, ch. 10, section 19. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/130102.htm

quotation.text: They are not different benefits but the same that the Apostle here wisheth, viz., the Holy Ghost: in partaking of the Holy Ghost, we possess and enjoy the love and grace of the Father and the Son, for the Holy Ghost is that love and grace...
quotation.edition: George P. Fisher (ed.), 'An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity' (1903), CCEL electronic edition
quotation.location: An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity, section on communion with God, p. 7 of the CCEL PDF
quotation.summary: Edwards reads the threefold benediction of 2 Corinthians 13:14 as one benefit, the Holy Ghost, in whom believers enjoy the love and grace of the Father and the Son.

explanation: Commenting on 'The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all' (2 Corinthians 13:14), Edwards argues that the three benefits named are not different benefits but the same: the Holy Ghost. In partaking of the Holy Ghost, believers possess and enjoy the love and grace of the Father and the Son, 'for the Holy Ghost is that love and grace'. The benediction is thus read as a summary of Edwards's whole account of the Trinity: the Son is God's idea, and the Spirit is the love in which Father and Son delight in each other.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Edwards reads 2 Corinthians 13:14 as naming one benefit - the Holy Ghost - in whom the love and grace of the Father and the Son are enjoyed. (A) The text names the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost. (B) The inference that the three are one benefit, the Spirit, is Edwards's, drawn from his identification of the Spirit with divine love. (D) 'The Holy Ghost is that love and grace' is Edwards's doctrinal formulation, not the Apostle's wording.
historicalContext: Discourse on the Trinity, begun early 1730, with additions in the mid- or late 1730s; unpublished in Edwards's lifetime and first published 1903. The essay is a private theological exercise, not a published doctrinal statement; it is recorded here as such.
citation: Jonathan Edwards, 'An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity', ed. George P. Fisher (1903); CCEL electronic edition, p. 7. Edition: George P. Fisher (ed.), 'An Unpublished Essay on the Trinity' (1903), CCEL electronic edition. URL: https://www.CCEL.ORG/ccel/e/edwards/trinity/cache/trinity.pdf. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: The quotation ends with an ellipsis: in the source the sentence continues '...and therefore I suppose it is that in that forementioned place, (I John 1:3). We are said to...'. No attested dissenting reading of 2 Corinthians 13:14 was located in the era sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty.

quotation.text: For it is He of whom the apostle says, But because you are sons, God has sent forth the Spirit of His Son into your hearts: and it is He of whom the same Son says, For it is not ye who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine cites Galatians 4:6 (the Spirit of the Son sent into our hearts) as evidence that the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, not of the Son alone or of the Father alone.

explanation: Augustine is arguing that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. He cites the apostle's words that God sent forth the Spirit of His Son into our hearts (Galatians 4:6), together with the Son's words that it is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matthew 10:20), to show that the same Spirit is called both the Spirit of the Son and the Spirit of the Father.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads Galatians 4:6 as showing that the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father. (A) The text states that God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying 'Abba! Father'. It does not state a doctrine of the Spirit's procession. (B) The step from the Spirit being called the Spirit of the Son to the Spirit's eternal procession from the Son is Augustine's inference. (D) The double-procession formulation is Augustine's own theological development, later disputed by the East (see john-of-damascus-john-15-26-001).
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book XV, chapter 26, where Augustine treats the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and from the Son.
citation: Augustine, On the Holy Trinity (De Trinitate), in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff, trans. Arthur West Haddan (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887), Book 15, ch. 26, section 45. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/130115.htm
notes: The quotation opens mid-sentence; the leading 'For it is He of whom the apostle says' is reproduced as printed. The inventory passage gal-4-4 is the sending of the Son (Gal. 4:4); Augustine's argument in this section is built on the immediately following verse, Gal. 4:6, and is recorded here as his reading of the sending passage's context.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 43, a. 2, sed contra, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1043.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether mission is eternal or only temporal. Against the claim that mission could be eternal, he cites Galatians 4:4: 'When the fullness of the time was come, God sent His Son.' Mission, for Aquinas, is the eternal procession with the addition of a temporal term: the Son is sent in time by becoming man (visible mission) and by dwelling in man by grace (invisible mission), while generation and spiration are exclusively eternal.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article belongs to q. 43 on the mission of the divine persons, distinguishing the eternal processions from the temporal missions.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 43, a. 2, sed contra
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites Galatians 4:4 ('God sent His Son' when the fullness of time was come) as the authority that mission is temporal, not eternal.
quotation.text: It is said (Galatians 4:4): "When the fullness of the time was come, God sent His Son."
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads Galatians 4:4 as showing that the Son's mission is temporal: God sent His Son when the fullness of time came. (A) The text states that God sent His Son, born of a woman, in the fullness of time; it does not distinguish mission from procession or use the scholastic vocabulary of eternal versus temporal terms. (D) The distinction between eternal procession and temporal mission is Aquinas's scholastic formulation and must not be presented as the wording of Galatians 4:4.

quotation.text: 'God sent forth His Son, made of a woman.' Christ therefore is true God and true man.
quotation.edition: Translated by Theodore Graebner (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1949)
quotation.location: Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, ch. 4, on Gal. 4:4-5, pp. 150-172
quotation.summary: Luther reads Galatians 4:4 as teaching that Christ is at once the Son of God and the son of a woman, and therefore true God and true man.

explanation: Commenting on 'God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law' (Galatians 4:4), Luther states: 'Christ therefore is true God and true man.' The verse joins the two natures: Christ is the Son of God and the son of a woman, and he submitted himself under the Law to redeem those who were under the Law. For Luther the point of the verse is redemption: the Son who is God became man under the Law in order to redeem us.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Luther reads Galatians 4:4 as teaching the two natures of Christ: true God (as the Son sent by God) and true man (as made of a woman). (A) The text says God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law. (B) The inference that 'Son of God' here proves Christ's deity, and 'made of a woman' his true humanity, is Luther's. (D) 'True God and true man' and 'two natures' are later doctrinal formulations applied to the text.
historicalContext: Commentary on Galatians, lectures delivered 1531, Latin commentary published 1535. Luther's exposition of chapter 4 treats the sending of the Son as the decisive act of redemption, in which the Son's divine origin and human birth are both affirmed.
citation: Martin Luther, A Commentary on St. Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, trans. Theodore Graebner (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1949), ch. 4, pp. 150-172. Edition: Translated by Theodore Graebner (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1949). URL: https://www.projectwittenberg.org/pub/resources/text/wittenberg/luther/gal/gal4-01.txt. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: No attested dissenting reading of Galatians 4:4 was located in the era sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty; this is absence of evidence in this pass, not a claim that no dissenting reading exists.

quotation.text: Have we not one God and one Christ and one Spirit of grace that was shed upon us? And is there not one calling in Christ?
quotation.edition: The Apostolic Fathers, trans. J. B. Lightfoot (repr. Grand Rapids, MI: Baker Book House, 1956)
quotation.location: First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, ch. 46
quotation.summary: Writing against schism at Corinth, Clement appeals to the shared 'one God, one Christ, one Spirit' and 'one calling in Christ' as the basis for unity - echoing the one body, one Spirit, and one calling of Ephesians 4:4.

explanation: In 1 Clement 46 Clement rebukes the Corinthians' strife: they who share one God, one Christ, and one Spirit of grace, and one calling, should not tear apart the members of Christ. The letter does not quote Ephesians 4:4 verbatim; the parallel is in the threefold 'one God, one Christ, one Spirit' and 'one calling.'
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Clement's threefold unity formula is consistent with, and likely echoes, Ephesians 4:4-6. The claim is a doctrinal connection (row B inference by the researcher), labelled as such: Clement does not cite Ephesians here, and the passage itself (row A) is about the one body, Spirit, hope, and calling. This is not a Trinitarian creed (row D).
historicalContext: First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, written c. 90-100 (range), is a letter from the church of Rome to the church of Corinth urging an end to the schism caused by the deposition of presbyters. Chapter 46 appeals to the Corinthians' shared unity as the ground for peace. The letter itself names no author; it is traditionally ascribed to Clement of Rome.
citation: Clement of Rome (traditionally ascribed), First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, ch. 46, in The Apostolic Fathers, trans. J. B. Lightfoot (repr. Grand Rapids, MI: Baker Book House, 1956); https://www.ccel.org/ccel/l/lightfoot/fathers/cache/fathers.txt (accessed 2026-11-20).
notes: The letter itself names no author; ascription to Clement of Rome is traditional. See the work entry (disputedAuthorship: true).

quotation.text: as being stones of the temple of the Father, prepared for the building of God the Father, and drawn up on high by the instrument of Jesus Christ, which is the cross, making use of the Holy Spirit as a rope, while your faith was the means by which you ascended, and your love the way which led up to God.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Ignatius pictures the Ephesians as stones of the Father's temple, lifted up by Christ the cross with the Holy Spirit as the rope, ascending to God - the threefold access of Ephesians 2:18, 'through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father,' joined to the temple imagery of Ephesians 2:19-22.

explanation: In Ephesians 9 Ignatius praises the Ephesians for stopping their ears to false doctrine: they are temple stones of the Father, raised by the instrument of Jesus Christ, the cross, using the Holy Spirit as a rope, with faith as the means of ascent and love as the way to God. Father, Christ, and Spirit each have a role in the one ascent to God.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): the threefold pattern - the Father's temple, Christ the instrument, the Spirit the rope - parallels Ephesians 2:18, though Ignatius does not quote the verse; the link is a doctrinal connection drawn by the researcher (row B). The Ephesians text (row A) speaks of access to the Father through Christ in one Spirit; the building-site metaphor is Ignatius's own.
historicalContext: Epistle to the Ephesians, written c. 105-115 (range) while Ignatius travelled under guard to Rome for martyrdom, exhorts the Ephesians to unity and warns against false teachers. Chapters 7 and 9 confess Christ and picture the believers' ascent to God.
citation: Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. 9, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0104.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: the blessed Apostle Paul teaches the same thing, and sets forth the sacrament of unity, saying, There is one body and one spirit, one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God?
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)
quotation.location: On the Unity of the Church, §4

explanation: Cyprian cites Ephesians 4:4-6 as Paul teaching 'the same thing' as the Lord's words about Peter and the one Church: one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. The sevenfold oneness of the passage is, for Cyprian, the scriptural statement of the sacrament of unity.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Cyprian reads Ephesians 4:4-6 as the apostolic statement of the unity that the Church must hold. (A) The passage names one Spirit, one Lord, and one God together, but does not name Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three persons, and does not state the Trinity. (D) Cyprian's use is ecclesiological (church unity grounded in divine unity), not a Nicene doctrinal formulation.
historicalContext: On the Unity of the Church, c. 251 (approximate), §4, written against the Novatian schism.
citation: Cyprian of Carthage, On the Unity of the Church, §§4, 6. Translated by Ernest Wallis. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886). New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050701.htm.
notes: No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task.

quotation.text: There is one Physician who is possessed both of flesh and spirit; both made and not made; God existing in flesh; true life in death; both of Mary and of God; first passible and then impassible - even Jesus Christ our Lord.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885)
quotation.summary: Warning against false teachers, Ignatius confesses one Physician, Jesus Christ, both made and not made, God existing in flesh, of Mary and of God - the pattern of Philippians 2:5-8, Christ in the form of God who took the form of a servant and was found in human likeness.

explanation: In Ephesians 7 Ignatius contrasts teachers who 'carry about the name' in guile with the one Physician: Jesus Christ, at once flesh and spirit, made and not made, God in flesh, passible then impassible. The paradoxical pairs confess the same twofold reality Paul states in Philippians 2: Christ Jesus, in the form of God, emptied himself and was found in human likeness.
relationshipToDoctrine: This is a historical reading (row C): Ignatius's confession is consistent with Philippians 2:5-8, though he does not quote the passage here; the link is a doctrinal connection drawn by the researcher (row B). The Philippians text (row A) speaks of Christ's form of God and form of a servant; Ignatius's 'God existing in flesh' is his own confessional phrasing, not later creedal language (row D).
historicalContext: Epistle to the Ephesians, written c. 105-115 (range) while Ignatius travelled under guard to Rome for martyrdom, exhorts the Ephesians to unity and warns against false teachers. Chapters 7 and 9 confess Christ and picture the believers' ascent to God.
citation: Ignatius of Antioch, Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. 7, in Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1, ed. Alexander Roberts, James Donaldson, and A. Cleveland Coxe (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0104.htm (accessed 2026-11-20).

quotation.text: For all these texts have the same force and meaning, a religious one, declarative of the divinity of the Word, even those of them which speak humanly concerning Him, as having become the Son of man.
quotation.translation: John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892)
quotation.location: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse II, Chapter XIV, section 1 (NPNF2 vol. 4, p. 348; New Advent §1)

explanation: Athanasius lists the texts the Arians misuse to call the Son a creature, including 'He emptied Himself, and took upon Him the form of a servant' (Philippians 2:7), alongside John 1:1, John 1:14, Acts 2:36, Proverbs 8:22, and Hebrews 1:4. He insists all these texts 'have the same force and meaning, a religious one, declarative of the divinity of the Word, even those of them which speak humanly concerning Him, as having become the Son of man': the lowly language belongs to the Word become man, not to the Word as a creature.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Athanasius reads Philippians 2:7 (within the Philippians 2:5-11 hymn) as speaking of the divine Word who became man, so that the self-emptying declares rather than denies his divinity. (D) The reading defends the Nicene settlement: the one who emptied himself is the eternal Word, not a creature exalted for foreseen virtue (the Arian reading).
historicalContext: Four Discourses Against the Arians, Discourse II, Chapter XIV, §1, c. 356-360 (range). The Arians argued from Proverbs 8:22 and Hebrews 3:2 that the Son is a work and a creature; Athanasius answers by re-reading the whole group of texts.
citation: Athanasius, Four Discourses Against the Arians. Translated by John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892). New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28161.htm (Discourse I); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28162.htm (Discourse II); https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/28164.htm (Discourse IV).
notes: The Arian reading of Philippians 2:7 (the Son as a creature exalted for foreseen virtue) is described generally in arius-john-1-1-001 and in the Arian controversy milestone; no Arian reading of Philippians 2 specifically was verified in the sources checked.

quotation.text: Paul does not disguise this, but openly exclaims, that 'being in the form of God (he) thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation'.
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 11
quotation.summary: Calvin reads Philippians 2:6 as Paul openly declaring Christ's equality with God before his self-emptying.

explanation: Calvin cites Philippians 2:6 as a proof of Christ's deity: Paul 'openly exclaims' that Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God. In Institutes I.xiii.24 Calvin returns to the passage to settle a dispute about Christ's subordination: 'the dispute is admirably settled by Paul, when he declares that he was equal with God before he humbled himself, and assumed the form of a servant.' The equality, on Calvin's reading, precedes the humbling, so the humbling is voluntary and does not prove inferiority of nature.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin reads Philippians 2:6 as asserting Christ's pre-existent equality with God. (A) The text says Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God. (B) The inference that equality with God proves Christ's deity is Calvin's. (D) 'Deity' and 'nature' are later doctrinal terms applied to the text.
historicalContext: Institutes I.xiii.11 and I.xiii.24, final edition 1559. In section 11 the verse is a proof of the Son's deity; in section 24 it settles a dispute with those who argued from Christ's humiliation to his inferiority.
citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, sections 11 and 24. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.

quotation.text: He is also styled First-born, as the apostle has declared: “who is the first-born of every creature.” The first-born, however, is not by nature a different person from the Wisdom, but one and the same.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885)

explanation: Origen identifies the Son under his many names: he is Wisdom (Proverbs 8:22), First-born (Colossians 1:15), and the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). The First-born is not a different person from the Wisdom, but one and the same: the only-begotten Son. In §5 he adds that Paul calls the Son 'the image of the invisible God' and 'the first-born of every creature'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Origen reads Colossians 1:15 as naming the Son 'first-born of every creature' while insisting he is one and the same person as the Wisdom, not a different being. (B) Origen's inference that 'first-born' does not make the Son a creature is his theological reading; the verse itself calls him first-born of creation, which Arians later used to argue the opposite. (D) Origen's account is pre-Nicene and subordinationist in places: the Son derives from the Father and is second to him, though Origen insists the generation is without beginning.
historicalContext: De Principiis, c. 220-230 (range), Book I, ch. 2, 'On Christ'. Origen is answering how the Son can be called Wisdom, Word, First-born, and image while remaining one person.
citation: Origen, De Principiis, Book I, ch. 2. Translated by Frederick Crombie. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4, ed. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Wikisource reproduction of ANF vol. 4: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Ante-Nicene_Fathers/Volume_IV/Origen/Origen_De_Principiis/I/Chapter_2.
notes: No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task. The Arian use of 'first-born of every creature' to argue the Son is a creature is recorded generally in arius-john-1-1-001 and in the Arian controversy milestone; no Arian reading of Colossians 1:15 specifically was verified in the sources checked.

quotation.text: for in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, and you are made full in Him, Which is the Head of all principality and power; […]
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 9 (1899)

explanation: Continuing his reading of Colossians 2:8-15 in §13, Hilary cites 'in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily' (Colossians 2:9) as the apostle's inspired teaching against 'philosophy and vain deceit'. Steadfast faith, he says, 'rejects the vain subtleties of philosophic enquiry' and refuses to confine God within the limits of common reason, because in Christ there is the fullness of the Godhead, and 'we must confess that Christ Jesus is none other than God in all the fullness of the Deity.' The ellipsis marks the continuation of the Colossians quotation.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Hilary reads Colossians 2:9 as Paul's statement that the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, and therefore that Christ Jesus is none other than God in all the fullness of the Deity. (D) The reading defends the post-Nicene faith against the Arian claim that the Son is a creature; it is Hilary's argument, not a quotation of the creed.
historicalContext: On the Trinity, Book I, §13, c. 356-359 (range), written in exile. The section warns against judging Christ 'after the rudiments of the world'.
citation: Hilary of Poitiers, On the Trinity, Book I. Translated by E. W. Watson. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 9, ed. Philip Schaff and Henry Wace (New York: The Christian Literature Company, 1899). New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/330201.htm.
notes: No dissenting reading of this passage from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked for this task.

quotation.text: And when writing to the Hebrews, he says of Him that He is “the brightness of His glory, and the express image of His person.”
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4 (1885)

explanation: Origen cites Hebrews 1:3 alongside Colossians 1:15 to support his account of the Son: the Son is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person, just as he is the image of the invisible God and the first-born of every creature. The image language lets Origen argue, in §6, that the image contains 'the unity of nature and substance belonging to Father and Son'.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Origen reads Hebrews 1:3 as Paul's description of the Son as the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person, and draws from the image analogy a unity of nature and substance between Father and Son. (B) The step from 'image' to 'unity of nature and substance' is Origen's inference. (D) Origen's 'unity of nature and substance' is his own pre-Nicene formulation, not the Nicene homoousios, and it sits alongside his subordination of the Son to the Father.
historicalContext: De Principiis, c. 220-230 (range), Book I, ch. 2, §§5-6.
citation: Origen, De Principiis, Book I, ch. 2. Translated by Frederick Crombie. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4, ed. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885). Wikisource reproduction of ANF vol. 4: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Ante-Nicene_Fathers/Volume_IV/Origen/Origen_De_Principiis/I/Chapter_2.

quotation.text: While he proclaims his unity, he distinctly sets it before us as existing in three persons.
quotation.edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845
quotation.location: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 1, Chapter 13, section 2
quotation.summary: Calvin states that the unity of God and his existence in three persons are taught together in Scripture, and that neither may be sacrificed to the other.

explanation: At the opening of Institutes I.xiii, Calvin states the doctrine he will defend: Scripture teaches at once the unity of God and that he exists in three persons. Hebrews 1:3 is the passage under discussion in section 2, where Calvin argues that the Son, as the brightness of the Father's glory, is distinct from the Father yet shares the divine being. The quotation is Calvin's summary of what Scripture proclaims, placed immediately after his citation of Hebrews 1:3.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin treats Hebrews 1:3 as a proof of the Son's distinct personhood within the one divine essence. (A) The text calls the Son the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person. (B) Calvin infers distinct subsistence with shared being from the image-language. (D) The formulation 'three persons' is later doctrinal vocabulary applied to the text, not its wording.
historicalContext: Institutes of the Christian Religion, final (fifth) Latin edition, 1559. Chapter 13 is Calvin's systematic defence of the Trinity, written against Arians, Sabellians, and the contemporary anti-Trinitarians (Servetus and others) who were active in Geneva and beyond in the 1550s.
citation: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, trans. Henry Beveridge, 2 vols. (Edinburgh: Calvin Translation Society, 1845), Book 1, Chapter 13, section 2. Edition: 1559 edition; Henry Beveridge translation, 1845. URL: https://www.calvinstitutes.org/book-1/1-13. Accessed 2026-11-20.
notes: No attested dissenting reading of Hebrews 1:3 was located in the era sources read in this pass, so alternativeReadings is empty; this is absence of evidence in this pass, not a claim that no dissenting reading exists.

quotation.text: The Lord says, I and the Father are one; and again it is written of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, And these three are one.
quotation.edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (1886)
quotation.location: On the Unity of the Church, §6

explanation: Arguing for the unity of the Church, Cyprian appeals to the unity of God: as the Lord says 'I and the Father are one', so 'it is written of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, And these three are one.' The sentence is cited in the Wallis translation with the footnote reference '1 John 5:7'. Cyprian uses the threefold unity as the pattern and ground of ecclesial unity.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Cyprian reads the words 'these three are one' as written of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and uses them as evidence of divine unity. (A) The wording Cyprian quotes resembles the later Johannine Comma ('For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one'), but Cyprian's sentence names the Father, the Son (not the Word), and the Holy Spirit, and does not quote the full Comma wording. Whether Cyprian knew a form of 1 John 5:7 containing the Comma is disputed; this record does NOT assert that the Comma is original to 1 John, and the Phase 2 finding stands that the Comma is not verified as original. (D) Cyprian predates Nicaea by about 75 years.
historicalContext: On the Unity of the Church, c. 251 (approximate), §6, written on the occasion of the schism of Novatian to recall the Carthaginians to unity. The treatise is about church unity, not a treatise on the Trinity; the trinitarian sentence serves the argument about unity.
citation: Cyprian of Carthage, On the Unity of the Church, §§4, 6. Translated by Ernest Wallis. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886). New Advent: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050701.htm.
notes: FLAG (textual history): Cyprian's 'And these three are one' is the earliest Latin witness sometimes cited in the Comma debate, but it is not a verbatim quotation of the Johannine Comma as it appears in the Textus Receptus/KJV (which names 'the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost' and speaks of bearing record in heaven). The Comma's originality is not verified (Phase 2: 1 not-verified record). No dissenting reading of 1 John 5:7 from a named writer in this era was verified in the sources checked.

quotation.text: And the same John most expressly affirms this in his epistle: For we know that the Son of God has come, and has given us an understanding, that we may know the true God, and that we may be in His true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff (1887)
quotation.summary: Augustine cites 1 John 5:20 as expressly affirming that Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, is the true God and eternal life.

explanation: Augustine cites 1 John 5:20 as the most express testimony that the Son is very God: John says the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may be in His true Son Jesus Christ, and then adds 'This is the true God, and eternal life', which Augustine takes to refer to Jesus Christ Himself.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads 1 John 5:20 as expressly affirming that Jesus Christ is the true God and eternal life. (A) The text states that we are in His true Son Jesus Christ and that 'This is the true God, and eternal life'; the referent of 'this' is debated, though Augustine takes it to be Christ. (B) Taking 'This is the true God' to refer to the Son is Augustine's reading of the verse's syntax. (D) The consubstantiality language is a later formulation applied to the text.
historicalContext: De Trinitate was written 399-422 (range; see works.json). Books I-IV defend the unity and equality of the Trinity from Scripture against those who argued, from texts about the sending and subordination of the Son and the Spirit, that the Son is less than the Father. This passage comes from Book I, chapter 6, where Augustine collects scriptural testimonies that the Son is very God, of the same substance with the Father.
citation: Augustine, On the Holy Trinity (De Trinitate), in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 3, ed. Philip Schaff, trans. Arthur West Haddan (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887), Book 1, ch. 6, section 9. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/130101.htm
notes: Augustine returns to the same verse in Contra Maximinum II.14.2-3, citing it again as proof that the Son is true God; that passage was checked but is recorded here as same-author corroboration only, not as a separate interpretation.

quotation.text: I would not have thee mistake that place in the epistle of John the apostle where he saith, 'There are three witnesses: the Spirit, and the water, and the blood: and the three are one.' Lest haply thou say that the Spirit and the water and the blood are diverse substances, and yet it is said, 'the three are one:' for this cause I have admonished thee, that thou mistake not the matter. For these are mystical expressions, in which the point always to be considered is, not what the actual things are, but what they denote as signs.
quotation.edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 7 (1888); Latin text Migne, Patrologia Latina 42.794-795
quotation.summary: Augustine quotes 1 John 5:7-8 in the form naming the earthly witnesses (Spirit, water, blood) and warns Maximinus not to mistake them for diverse substances, since they are mystical expressions to be understood by what they signify.

explanation: Maximinus had cited 1 John 5:7-8 to argue that the Father and the Son are not one substance, since the Spirit, the water, and the blood are said to be one although they are diverse things. Augustine replies that the verse names three witnesses, the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and that these are mystical expressions: the point is not what the actual things are, but what they denote as signs. He then reads them as signifying the Trinity - the Spirit signifying the Father, the blood the Son, and the water the Holy Spirit - so that 'There are Three Witnesses, and the Three are One' can be said of them too.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Augustine reads the three witnesses of 1 John 5:7-8 allegorically as signifying the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. (A) The verse names the Spirit, the water, and the blood and says the three are one; it does not name the persons of the Trinity. (B) The allegorical identification of the three witnesses with the three persons is Augustine's reading, not the text's claim. (D) The doctrine of the Trinity is not stated by the verse. TEXTUAL DISPUTE: Augustine's text of 1 John 5:7-8 contains only the earthly witnesses (Spirit, water, blood). The heavenly-witnesses clause (the 'Comma Johanneum' - the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost) does not appear in his text; the same source page's footnote 56 states that the clause 'appears to be wholly unknown to St. Augustin'. The Comma is therefore NOT asserted here as original.
historicalContext: Contra Maximinum was written 427-428 (range), shortly after Augustine's public debate at Hippo with Maximinus, a Homoian Arian bishop. In Book II, chapter 22, Augustine answers Maximinus's use of 1 John 5:7-8 against the unity of substance of Father and Son.
citation: Augustine, Answer to Maximinus the Arian (Contra Maximinum), Book II, ch. 22, section 3. In Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series I, Vol. 7, Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Part 11, trans. H. Browne (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1888). Latin text in Migne, Patrologia Latina 42.794-795. https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nicene_and_Post-Nicene_Fathers:_Series_I/Volume_VII/First_Epistle_of_John/Part_11

The heavenly-witnesses clause (Comma Johanneum) does not appear in his text; the source page's editor footnote 56 states the clause 'appears to be wholly unknown to St. Augustin'. The Comma must not be asserted as original on the basis of this passage. EDITION CONFIRMED (Phase 5): the English text is the H. citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 27, a. 1, respondeo, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1027.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas argues that procession in God must be understood as an inward, intelligible procession, not an outward movement. He rejects the Arian reading, under which the Son proceeds from the Father as His primary creature, because it contradicts 1 John 5:20: the Son is 'true God'. The verse is used as the proof that the Son who proceeds is truly God, not a creature.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article opens the Trinitarian treatise by establishing that there is procession in God, against Arius (who made the Son a creature) and Sabellius (who denied real distinction).

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 27, a. 1, respondeo
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites 1 John 5:20 ('This is true God') against the Arian reading that the Son proceeds as a creature: the Son who proceeds is true God.
quotation.text: In this sense neither the Son nor the Holy Ghost would be true God: and this is contrary to what is said of the Son, "That . . . we may be in His true Son. This is true God" (1 John 5:20).
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads 1 John 5:20 as stating that the Son is 'true God', and uses it to reject the Arian reading of the Son's procession as creaturely. (A) The text states that Jesus Christ 'is the true God and eternal life'; it does not use the language of procession or of the Son's relation to the Father. (D) The scholastic account of procession as an inward intelligible emanation is Aquinas's formulation and must not be presented as the wording of 1 John 5:20.

citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 36, a. 1, sed contra, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent, https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1036.htm (accessed 2026-11-20). Print: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (London: Burns Oates & Washbourne, 1920; repr. New York: Benziger Bros., 1947-48).
explanation: Aquinas asks whether 'Holy Ghost' is the proper name of one divine person. He answers yes, citing 1 John 5:7 ('There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost') as the scriptural naming of three, and Augustine's 'Three persons' as the answer to 'Three what?'. For Aquinas, the verse names the Holy Ghost as one of the three persons. TEXTUAL FLAG: 1 John 5:7 in this form is the Johannine Comma, absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and omitted in modern critical editions (the ESV omits it; the KJV includes it). Aquinas, like the medieval Latin tradition generally, cites the verse as it stood in the Latin Vulgate text he used. The Comma must not be asserted as original to John's epistle; what is recorded here is Aquinas's medieval use of the verse as he received it.
historicalContext: Written as part of the Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, composed 1265-1268 (whole work composed 1265-1274; certainty: range). The article opens Aquinas's treatment of the person of the Holy Ghost (q. 36), in a Latin tradition that read 1 John 5:7 with the Comma as part of the biblical text.
notes: TEXTUAL DISPUTE FLAGGED: the Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7) is not original to the epistle on the evidence of the earliest Greek manuscripts; modern critical editions omit it. Aquinas cites it as Scripture because it stood in the Vulgate text he used. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), Canon 2, likewise quotes 1 John 5:7-8, adding of v. 8 'as it is found in some codices'. Do not present the Comma as original.

quotation.edition: English translation by the Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920), New Advent online edition
quotation.location: Summa Theologiae I, q. 36, a. 1, sed contra
quotation.summary: Aquinas cites 1 John 5:7 as naming the three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, to show that 'Holy Ghost' is the proper name of one divine person. The verse as cited is the Johannine Comma, which is textually disputed (see notes).
quotation.text: It is said (1 John 5:7): "There are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost."
quotation.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province

relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Aquinas reads 1 John 5:7 as naming the Holy Ghost as one of three persons who bear witness in heaven, and takes it as scriptural warrant that 'Holy Ghost' is the proper name of one divine person. (A) The verse as Aquinas cites it names Father, Word, and Holy Ghost as three witnesses; the Comma's originality is disputed (see notes) and must not be asserted. (D) The scholastic account of 'Holy Ghost' as the proper name of the person proceeding by way of love is Aquinas's formulation and must not be presented as the wording of the verse.

quotation.text: But as even the Greek copies do not agree, I dare not assert any thing on the subject. Since, however, the passage flows better when this clause is added, and as I see that it is found in the best and most approved copies, I am inclined to receive it as the true reading.
quotation.edition: Calvin's Commentaries, Vol. 45: Catholic Epistles; tr. John King, 1847-50
quotation.location: Commentary on the Catholic Epistles, 1 John 5:7 (Vol. 45)
quotation.summary: Calvin is tentative about the Johannine Comma: the Greek copies disagree, so he will not assert anything; but because the passage flows better with the clause and it stands in the best copies, he is inclined to receive it as the true reading.

explanation: Calvin comments on the disputed words of 1 John 5:7 ('the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one'). He notes that some copies omit the verse, that Jerome thought the omission was deliberate on the part of the Latins, and that the Greek copies do not agree, so he 'dare not assert any thing on the subject'. He is nevertheless inclined to receive the clause as the true reading because the passage flows better with it and it is found in the best and most approved copies. He adds that 'These three are one' refers 'not to essence, but on the contrary to consent', as though the Father, the eternal Word, and the Spirit harmoniously testify the same thing respecting Christ. The dispute about the verse's authenticity is therefore recorded in Calvin's own words, and his position is tentative, not dogmatic.
relationshipToDoctrine: (C) Calvin tentatively receives the disputed clause of 1 John 5:7 as the true reading, while admitting he cannot assert anything about it, and reads 'these three are one' as consent in testimony rather than unity of essence. (A) The disputed text says there are three that bear record in heaven, and these three are one. (B) Calvin's inference from the better flow of the passage to the clause's genuineness is his own judgment. (D) The doctrinal use of the verse as a proof of the Trinity is later application, and Calvin himself warns against pressing 'are one' into a statement of essence.
historicalContext: Commentary on the Catholic Epistles, published 1551, Geneva. Calvin writes at a time when the verse's authenticity was already disputed among scholars; his caution is part of his general practice of refusing to over-claim from a doubtful text.

alternativeReadings.summary: The Racovian Catechism notes that the words of 1 John 5:7 'are wanting in most of the older Greek copies' and lists the verse among the testimonies that prove only the association of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in divine things, not three persons in one essence; see the racovian-catechism-1605 milestone.
